measures.what_it_does: Repeals the 9.9% tax on Washington taxable income above $1 million that the Legislature passed in 2026 (ESSB 6346), which would first apply to 2028 income, and adds a state law barring the state, counties, cities and all other local governments from taxing individual income or taxing by a measure of it. The sales tax, B&O tax and Working Families Tax Credit changes passed with the tax are not repealed.
measures.cost_line: OFM estimates $11.4 billion less state revenue over fiscal years 2027-2031, mostly from the general fund that pays for K-12, higher education and human services, including $377 million that would have gone to child care and early learning; agency savings of about $150 million; no effect on local revenue.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (State Sen. Chris Gildon, a retired Seattle firefighter/paramedic and small business owners) says voters have rejected an income tax ten times, that lawmakers left the door open to extend this one below $1 million, and that the Legislature has repeatedly shifted dedicated funds; it says the tax relief passed with the tax would stay in place.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Washington Education Association President Janie White, Washington State Labor Council President April Sims, a nurse, a teacher, a brewery owner and a Planned Parenthood Advocates representative) says the repeal is a tax break for the top 1% that would cut funding for schools, health care and childcare, and that the tax cuts for working families and small businesses depend on this revenue.

taxes.basis: YES repeals a 9.9% tax on income over $1 million (OFM: $11.4 billion in state revenue over SFY 2027-2031) and bars any future state or local income tax by statute: the rubric's 'limit & cut taxes' pole against its named 'millionaires tax' example of the other pole.

local-control.basis: YES writes one statewide rule that binds 'the state, counties, cities, and all other local jurisdictions', taking the income-tax option away from every local government (a state limit on local authority, the regional/state-standards pole). Strength 1, not 2: RCW 1.90.100 (I-2111) already bars local income taxes and ESSB 6346 left that ban in place for local governments, so the change for cities and counties is a re-enactment in broader terms.

spending.basis: The yes case rests on fiscal restraint and accountability (fund transfers, unkept spending commitments, 'demonstrate they can keep the commitments') while the no case and OFM tie the revenue to K-12, health care, childcare and free school meals; YES removes revenue the Legislature meant for those expansions. Strength 1 because the measure itself contains no audit or spending rule and the effect runs through revenue.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title, AG explanatory statement, OFM fiscal impact statement, pro/con statements and complete text (S1-S5); AG public investment impact disclosure (S6); House Office of Program Research summary (S7); ESSB 6346 session law (S8); RCW 1.90.100 (S9); PDC committee and contribution data for No on 645, Vote Yes Repeal the Income Tax and Let's Go Washington (S11-S14); litigation coverage (S15-S18); endorsements (S19-S24).

measures.what_it_does: Restores the state's list of parents' rights in public schools (RCW 28A.605.005) to the version enacted by Initiative 2081 in 2024, undoing the Legislature's 2025 rewrite in ESHB 1296. Parents would get school records, including health and counseling records, within 10 business days instead of up to 45 days; prior notice when a school offers medical services; and wider opt-outs from surveys, assignments and activities. Several entries in the 2025 version (nondiscrimination, bullying complaints, enrollment, language access, special education) would leave the list, the nondiscrimination entry being replaced by an assurance against discrimination based on the family's religious beliefs, and records protection in abuse cases would narrow to medical, health and counseling records during an investigation of the parent.
measures.cost_line: OFM: no fiscal impact on state government and no effect on state or local revenue; school districts may have minor costs to update policies and procedures, amount indeterminate.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (two teachers who serve as union representatives, the La Center School District superintendent, a parent and education advocate, a women's rights advocate and a member of Democrats for an Informed Approach to Gender) says it restores parents' access to materials, records and medical notices, that safeguards for at-risk children should not become a default of withholding information from all parents, and that schools should not keep a child's new gender identity at school from parents.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (State Sen. John Lovick, the presidents of the Washington State Nurses Association and the League of Women Voters of Washington, a school counselor, and representatives of the state domestic violence coalition and Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates) says it would open sensitive records to parents under investigation for harming their child, weaken immediate notice when a child is a crime victim at school, and discourage students, including LGBTQ+ students, from seeking help from school staff.

parental-rights.basis: YES restores I-2081's notification, records and opt-out rights: copies of all student-specific records, including health and mental health counseling records, within 10 business days; prior notice of school-offered medical services; opt-outs from any survey, assignment or activity touching sexual experience, family beliefs or mental health; and removes the 'in accordance with policies and procedures' qualifier on curriculum access. That is the rubric's pole A ('Parental notification and opt-out', -2). The 2025 law it replaces kept FERPA's 45-day standard, chapter 70.02 RCW health-record confidentiality and federal-scope opt-outs, which is pole B. Strength 2: the measure's whole subject is this list, and nearly every change on notice, records and opt-outs moves toward pole A (the exception is crime notice, which moves from 'upon receipt of a report' to when a criminal action 'is deemed to have been committed', while dropping the on-campus limit); the entries it drops (enrollment, language access, special education, bullying complaints) are not notification or opt-out rights, and the AG says the 2025 list restated many rights found elsewhere in law.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title, AG explanatory statement, OFM fiscal impact statement, pro/con statements and complete text (S1-S5); House Office of Program Research summary (S6); ESHB 1296 session law, 2025 c 369 (S7); Initiative 2081 legislative history (S8); current RCW 28A.605.005 (S9); PDC data for Let's Go Washington and No Hate in WA State (S10-S13); endorsements and coverage (S14-S21). Not mapped to social: the text's only gender-identity reference is the 2025 nondiscrimination entry it strikes from the list, while RCW 28A.642.010 itself is unchanged (dossier Axis notes).

measures.what_it_does: Requires school district and WIAA rules to bar students the measure calls "biologically male" from girls-only interschool competitions, individual or team, at public K-12 schools and private schools in the WIAA. Every student entering a girls-only competition would need a statement from her own health care provider, as part of the sports physical, verifying biological sex based on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels. It replaces the current WIAA rule that students compete consistent with their gender identity.
measures.cost_line: OFM: about $21,000 one time for OSPI to update guidance; school districts may incur indeterminate costs to revise policies; no effect on state or local revenue. OFM does not estimate costs to families for verification.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (a coach, an Olympic medalist, a pediatrician, a student athlete, a parent and education advocate, and a member of Democrats for an Informed Approach to Gender) says it protects fairness in girls' sports and the rights established by Title IX, aligns Washington with federal law and international sports bodies, and that verification can happen during routine, non-invasive primary care.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (the presidents of the Washington State Nurses Association and the League of Women Voters of Washington, a family physician, a retired school nurse, a girls' wrestling coach and Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates) says it would subject girls, and only girls, to intrusive medical sex verification, burden families without a regular doctor, and bar the 5 to 10 transgender girls in school sports with no case-by-case decisions.

social.basis: YES writes sex-based eligibility into law for girls' interscholastic sports, with provider verification of biological sex for every girl entering a female-only competition, replacing WIAA Rule 18.16.0 (participation by gender identity). The rubric's social pole A (-2) names 'Sex-based eligibility for girls' and women's sports' and pole B names 'Trans participation in sports by gender identity'. Strength 2: this is the measure's only subject.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title, AG explanatory statement, OFM fiscal impact statement, pro/con statements and complete text (S1-S5); House Office of Program Research summary (S6); WIAA 2026-27 Handbook (S7); WIAA amendment vote coverage (S8); West Virginia v. B. P. J. (S9); PDC data for Let's Go Washington and No Hate in WA State (S10-S12); endorsements and coverage (S13-S19). Not mapped to local-control: the measure swaps one statewide eligibility standard for another rather than moving the decision between levels of government (dossier Axis notes).

measures.what_it_does: Annexes the City of Bothell into the Shoreline Fire Department Regional Fire Authority effective March 1, 2027, so the Bothell Fire Department becomes part of the regional authority, whose nine-member board would include three Bothell City Councilmembers.
measures.cost_line: The ballot title gives no rate. Starting in 2028, Bothell property would pay the RFA levy (expected at about $0.45 per $1,000, with authority up to $1.00) plus a fire benefit charge. City staff estimate about $72 more a month for an average $945,000 home, or about $33 a month if the council cuts the city levy as it says it intends to.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Wesley Wang, Brandon Keith, and Mason Thompson) says regional fire service is the standard model, that joining lets Bothell share resources and future facility costs across a larger tax base, and that Bothell keeps 'a substantial voice' with three of nine RFA board seats. It notes the endorsement of IAFF Local 2099.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed. No one contacted King County Elections to serve on the con committee, and the city reports no con-committee applicants.

local-control.basis: YES moves fire and EMS governance from the Bothell City Council to a nine-member regional fire authority board on which Bothell holds three seats. That board sets the RFA levy and fire benefit charge and may amend the plan's finance section.

taxes.basis: YES adds the RFA property-tax levy and fire benefit charge to Bothell property from 2028. City staff estimate a net increase of about $33 a month for an average home, even after the council's intended (non-binding) cut to the city levy, and about $72 a month without that cut.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1) and the statement for, with no statement against filed (S2). City of Bothell July 21, 2026 agenda bill, Resolution 1784 and the amended RFA Plan, with fiscal estimates (S3). City Fire Service Study page (S4). Shoreline Fire RFA FAQ for Bothell and Sno10 (S5). Shoreline Area News (S6). PDC committee search (S7).

measures.what_it_does: A levy lid lift that raises Clyde Hill's regular property tax to keep paying for police, fire and EMS, 911 dispatch, and land use and zoning services. The ballot title says its purpose is for Clyde Hill to remain an independent city; after 2036 the higher levy becomes the permanent base.
measures.cost_line: Raises the levy from $0.29548 to up to $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027, then lets the levy amount grow 3% a year from 2028 to 2036; the city estimates about $225 more per $1,000,000 of assessed value (about $900 on a $4 million home).
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Jay Henningsen, Carl Picciotto, Tony Williams) says rising costs and state limits on revenue have opened a budget gap that cuts alone cannot close. It calls the lift a modest increase recommended by a resident task force that keeps the city's accredited police department and its control over land use.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed. The pamphlet says the opposition committee withdrew from writing one.

taxes.basis: A new, large and permanent increase: the city's rate rises from $0.29548 to up to $0.50 per $1,000 (a 69-72% increase in the city's share), followed by 3% annual growth for nine years and a permanent new base after 2036.

local-control.basis: The ballot title says the measure's purpose is 'to remain an independent city.' The explanatory statement says that without it the city cannot keep 'local control of its police department and zoning issues' and 'may need to consider dissolution,' and the city and task force name merging with a neighbor or contracting out police as the alternatives. YES keeps these decisions with the smallest local unit. Strength is 1 rather than 2 because a NO vote does not itself dissolve or merge the city; the task force's first fallback is to resubmit the levy.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); pro statement and rebuttal, plus the note that the opposition committee withdrew (S2); Resolution No. 725 (S3); city levy page and FAQ (S4, S5); Financial Sustainability Task Force final report and levy recommendation (S6, S7); staff reports including the Raftelis analysis (S8, S9); PDC committee summary (S10); pro committee site (S11); The Urbanist and a Seattle Times column (S12, S13). Spending is omitted because the resolution limits the money to existing service levels.

measures.what_it_does: Lets Issaquah issue up to $18 million in 20-year general obligation bonds, repaid by a property tax levy, for park projects from the 2024 Park System Plan: turf sports fields opened to the community, new trails on Cougar and Squak mountains, a trailhead upgrade, the Ek House restoration, a new playground and dog park, and pickleball courts. The new bonds would replace the city's retiring park bonds.
measures.cost_line: Authorizes up to $18,000,000 in bonds maturing within 20 years, repaid by annual excess property taxes. The city says the bonds would be issued as earlier park bonds mature, keeping the levy at about 8 cents per $1,000; it estimates about $80 a year on a $1 million home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Jeffrey Newell, Robin Beukers, Donovan Richards) calls the measure a renewal rather than a new tax. It says years of planning and community input chose its fields, trails, playground, dog park and Ek House projects, and that without it they could take more than 30 years to finish.
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Steve Pereira) does not object to the specific projects. It argues the city should first rank projects against the park plan's goals and level-of-service benchmarks before committing 20 years of park bonding capacity, and asks voters to vote 'Not yet.'

taxes.basis: New 20-year bond debt sized to replace retiring park bonds and keep the levy near its current 8 cents per $1,000 (about $80 a year on a $1 million home); a replacement at a similar rate.

spending.basis: Pays for new park capacity, not just upkeep: new trail corridors and more than 35 acres of open space, a new dog park and playground, new pickleball courts, and school fields turfed and opened for year-round community use.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); pro/con statements and rebuttals (S2); Ordinance No. 3142, which records the 2006 and 2013 bond history and retirement dates (S3); city park bond page, read through a reader proxy because the site blocks automated requests (S4); PDC committee registration (S5). No news coverage was found.

measures.what_it_does: Lifts Kenmore's regular property-tax levy lid to fund climate and environmental stewardship, affordable housing (through ARCH), and human services, as the city's first levy lid lift. The higher 2032 levy becomes the permanent base for later years.
measures.cost_line: Raises the levy by about $0.36 per $1,000 of assessed value, to a total rate not to exceed $1.25 per $1,000 for collection in 2027, with up to 6% annual increases in 2028-2032. The city estimates about $30 a month for a home assessed at $1,000,000. Qualifying seniors, veterans and people with disabilities are exempt.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Tracy Banaszynski, Edouard Lassalle, and Juliana Pooley) says Prop 1 funds trees, greenspace and climate readiness, affordable homes through ARCH, and help with food, utilities and health care. It says the levy keeps services going despite a 1% cap while costs rose about 5% a year, and that 'Cutting resiliency programs doesn't save money.'
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Laurie Sperry, John Hendrickson, and Dave Postetter) says the city tax rate rises over 51% in 2027 and permanently becomes the base for more increases. It says city spending grew more than 40% since 2020 while population grew 1.6%, and that the council can shift funds among uses without voter approval.

taxes.basis: YES raises the city levy by about $0.36 on a stated current rate of $0.70 per $1,000, allows 6% annual growth through 2032, and makes the 2032 amount the permanent base: a large, permanent increase. The con case centers on resisting it.

spending.basis: YES funds city climate, housing (ARCH) and human-services programs that staff costed as 'Enhanced + Special Projects.' The pro case frames this as investing in resiliency programs; the con case argues it backfills the general fund.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1), and the pro and con statements and rebuttals (S2). Ordinance 26-0644 and the June 15, 2026 agenda packet (S3) and minutes (S4). May 4, 2026 study-session scenarios (S5) and minutes (S6). City Prop 1 page and FAQs (S7). Shoreline Area News (S8). Pro and con committee sites (S9, S10). PDC committee record (S11).

measures.what_it_does: A six-year levy lid lift that raises Lake Forest Park's regular property tax to pay for police, 911 dispatch, emergency management, jail, prosecution and public defense, and mental health crisis response. The added money is tracked separately and may only be spent on these public safety services.
measures.cost_line: Sets the city's maximum regular levy rate at $0.88920 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 (up $0.22 from $0.66920), with annual increases tied to Seattle-area inflation (CPI-U) through 2032; the city estimates about $211.86 a year ($17.66 a month) on the $963,000 median home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Marty Ross) says the state's 1% cap on property tax growth has not kept up with inflation, that city staff project the general fund will run out by 2031 under the status quo, and that the council voted unanimously to send the levy to voters.
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (T.J. Fudge) says the author supports more money for public safety, but the city has not committed to adding the levy on top of current general-fund spending on public safety. It also says the city exaggerates its budget problems while adding non-safety staff.

taxes.basis: A new levy increase, not a renewal: it raises the city's regular levy rate by about a third ($0.66920 to $0.88920 per $1,000, about $1.25 million a year), with CPI-U increases for five more years. A nearly identical 2025 measure failed by 19 votes.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); pro/con statements (S2); Resolution No. 26-2084 with Attachment A (S3); city levy page and FAQ (S4, S5); VoteWA results for the failed November 2025 measure (S6); Shoreline Area News coverage and republished city announcements (S7-S10); PDC committee summary (S11); pro committee site (S12, S13). Spending is omitted because the resolution limits the money to maintaining existing service levels.

measures.what_it_does: Raises Milton's sales and use tax by 0.1% starting in 2027 to fund police and public safety under RCW 82.14.450. It has no expiration date, and 15% of the proceeds go to the county.
measures.cost_line: Increases the sales and use tax rate by one-tenth of one percent (0.001), or 10 cents on a $100 taxable purchase; the city estimates about $200,000 a year. Combined rates would go from 10.3% to 10.4% in the King County part of Milton and from 10.2% to 10.3% in the Pierce County part.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Dave Strader, Jacki Strader) says the tax will let the Milton Police Department 'maintain its current budget and high-quality services' as staffing, jail, court and other costs rise. It says the tax will ease pressure on the General Fund and protect funding for streets and parks.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed. No one volunteered for the opposition committee, and the council found no 'Against' volunteers when it appointed committees.

taxes.basis: A yes vote creates a new 0.1% public safety sales tax with no expiration date. Neither King nor Pierce County currently levies this tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1) and statement in favor (S2); VoteWA record showing the Pierce County administration (S3); Milton council packets with the staff report, budget figures, Resolution 26-2005 and the 6-0 adoption vote (S4, S5); DOR Q4 2026 rates (S6); RCW 82.14.450 (S7); PDC query showing no committees (S8). No news coverage was found.

measures.what_it_does: Raises SeaTac's sales and use tax by 0.1% to fund fire, emergency medical, law enforcement and criminal justice services. The tax has no expiration date; 85% of the revenue goes to the city and 15% to King County.
measures.cost_line: Increases the city's sales and use tax rate by 1/10th of 1% (0.1%), which 'would add $0.10 to a taxable $100 purchase'. The combined rate would go from 10.4% to 10.5%. The city expects about $2 million a year, of which it keeps $1.7 million.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (James Lovell, Damiana Merryweather) says the tax spreads public safety costs to the thousands of workers, travelers and airport users who make taxable purchases in SeaTac. It also says acting before King County keeps a larger share of the revenue under local control.
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Susan Constable) cites the city's 2014 utility tax and its 2015 repeal. It argues the council has a spending problem, calls the new B&O tax 'a red flag', and says these taxes are regressive and that airline tickets are exempt from sales tax.

taxes.basis: A yes vote creates a new 0.1% public safety sales tax with no expiration date, expected to raise about $2 million a year. It comes on top of a separate B&O tax due in 2027.

measures.sources_note: Sources: pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); statements and rebuttals (S2); Ordinance 26-1017 with the deficit and revenue recitals (S3); RCW 82.14.450 (S4); DOR Q4 2026 rate (S5); PDC filings for Yes for SeaTac Safety (S6, S7); SeaTac Blog coverage of the council vote, the B&O tax, and the 2014-2015 utility tax (S8-S11). The city website blocked automated access.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes a Seattle sales and use tax of up to 0.3% for up to ten years (April 2027-March 2037) to replace the expiring 0.15% Seattle Transit Measure. The money would buy more King County Metro bus service, transit safety and security staff, free and reduced-fare transit passes, streetcar operations, transit capital projects and City staffing for Sound Transit 3, with at least 75% going to bus service and transit safety and security.
measures.cost_line: Authorizes "a 0.3% sales and use tax for up to ten years to replace the current voter-approved 0.15% sales tax expiring March 31, 2027" (no vehicle license fee). The City estimates about $138 million a year on average. SDOT estimates the full 0.3% tax costs a two-person median-income household about $58 a year; the campaign says the increase is "$29 more per year per household." Seattle's combined sales tax rate would rise from 10.55% to 10.7%, or 10.8% counting the separate 0.1% county roads tax that starts in January 2027.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Kirk Hovenkotter, Kathryn Ricchiuto, Nick Sattele) says the 2020 measure delivered more frequent buses and 10,000 free transit passes, and its funding runs out in 2027 unless renewed. It says that for "$29 more per year per household" buses will come more often, later at night and on weekends, and free passes for low-income residents will double, helping families avoid the cost of gas or a second car.
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Ari Hoffman) says the measure doubles a regressive sales tax, bringing Seattle's rate to 10.7%, at a time of high living costs. It objects to funding connected to Sound Transit and to uncollected fares, and says City Hall should prioritize existing resources and improve fare collection before raising taxes.

taxes.basis: A yes vote doubles the dedicated transit sales tax from 0.15% to up to 0.3% (the statutory maximum) for up to ten years. Average revenue would be $138M a year ($1.38B total) versus $56.6M under the current rate, and the Council rejected a smaller 0.225% option. This is a replacement at a doubled rate.

spending.basis: A yes vote funds an expansion of programs beyond current service: about 95,000-100,000 more Metro trips or service hours a year, free ORCA passes rising from about 10,000 to 22,000, and a new transit safety and security category, with at least 75% of revenue reserved for service.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1), pro/con statements and rebuttals (S2), and full ordinance text (S3); signed Ordinance 127474 (S4), Legistar history (S5), Council minutes of July 21, 2026 (S6), Central Staff memo (S7), SDOT fiscal note (S8), committee amendment tally and packets (S9-S11), Council topic page (S12), DOR rate lookup (S13), PDC committee and contribution data (S14-S15), the pro campaign website (S16), and coverage from The Urbanist, The Seattle Times, KUOW and PubliCola (S17-S25).

measures.what_it_does: Creates the Shoreline Metropolitan Park District, a new taxing district with the city's boundaries and governed by the City Councilmembers, to build, operate and maintain a new indoor pool facility (about $100 million) and possible future recreation facilities.
measures.cost_line: Levies up to $0.75 per $1,000 of assessed value, with an anticipated initial rate of $0.55 per $1,000 (about $8.8 million a year) starting in 2028. The city estimates about $421 a year ($35 a month) for a median-value home ($831,000 in 2026).
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Krishnakant Nammi, Susie McDowell, and Buddy Smith) says a local pool would provide swim lessons that reduce drowning risk, a home for school swim teams, and aquatic exercise for seniors. It says residents shouldn't have to leave town, and that the measure replaces the pool Shoreline had from 1971 to 2020.
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Sandra Cribbs, Jeff Hays, and Joseph Smith) calls it a permanent tax increase of at least 33% of city property taxes for a '$100 million luxury pool' with no recreation or senior center. It says the new district would get authority to fund future projects without going back to voters.

taxes.basis: YES creates a new junior taxing district with permanent regular property-tax authority ($0.55 initial, $0.75 cap, about $8.8 million a year). The con case centers on resisting a permanent new tax.

spending.basis: YES funds a new roughly $100 million aquatic facility and ongoing operating subsidy, restoring a public pool Shoreline has lacked since 2020 and enabling future recreation facilities. This is public investment to expand amenities.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1), and the pro and con statements and rebuttals (S2). City of Shoreline Prop 1 page (S3). Shoreline Area News and Puget Sound Business Journal coverage of cost, council vote and pool history, including the failed 2019 bond (S4-S9). Pro and con committee sites (S10-S12). PDC committee totals (S13).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes Auburn School District to issue up to $491 million in 20-year bonds to build a new Middle School #5 and replace Cascade Middle School and Alpac Elementary with larger schools. The same three schools were in bonds that failed to reach the required 60% in 2024 (a larger $532.1 million package, 55%) and 2025 ($490 million, 54%).
measures.cost_line: Up to $491,000,000 in bonds repaid by excess property taxes. The district estimates an average of $1.10 per $1,000 of assessed value, about $55 a month on a $600,000 home. The district's own projections for these bonds run from $0.93 in 2027 to $1.61 per $1,000 in 2041-2048.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Cari Manry, Terri Herren) says the bond would end middle-school overcrowding (more than 1,100 students in 45 portables), replace aging buildings at about $1.10 per $1,000, and secure state matching funds, noting that a majority voted yes last time.
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Eric Petersen) says $163 million per school is excessive next to Tacoma's costs, and that repaying principal plus $350+ million in interest pushes the real rate to $1.93 per $1,000; it asks voters to make the district resubmit a smaller request.

taxes.basis: A yes vote authorizes a new $491 million bond, not a renewal. The district projects its combined bond rate rising from $1.50 (2026) to $2.53 (2027-2031) and $2.65 (2032-2039) per $1,000; the con case is about tax burden.

spending.basis: Beyond replacing two schools, the bond builds a fifth middle school to increase capacity and reduce class sizes and portable use; the opposition argues for a smaller, cheaper request.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1) and statements (S2); district election page, Q&A and Election Information Book with Resolution 1426 history and debt service projections (S3-S5); district 2025 bond page (S6); Auburn Reporter coverage of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 bonds (S7-S9); PDC records for Auburn Citizen's for Schools (S10-S11).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes Highline School District to issue $595.4 million in bonds (up to 21 years) to replace Sylvester and Cascade middle schools, partly rebuild Chinook Middle School, rebuild the Southern Heights site for CHOICE Academy, fund $40 million in districtwide critical repairs, and design future Hilltop and Valley View projects.
measures.cost_line: $595,400,000 in general obligation bonds repaid by excess property taxes. The district does not publish a rate for this bond alone; its table of total bond rates (existing plus proposed) shows $2.30 per $1,000 in 2026 and $2.36, $2.32, $2.28 and $2.25 in 2027-2030. For this bond and Prop. 2 together the district projects the total school tax rate going from $4.47 to $4.89 per $1,000, about $210 a year ($17.50 a month) on a $500,000 home; most of that increase is the Prop. 2 levy.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Tina Orwall, Dan Satterberg, Sili Savusa, www.yesforHighline.org) says the bond replaces aging, unsafe middle schools so every neighborhood has a modern school, avoids costlier repairs later, and was shaped by a community-led advisory committee, with Highline delivering past projects on time and on budget.
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Mike Bishoff, Kirsten Cooper, Katie Paulson, BetterPlanforHighline.com) says a 'record-breaking' bond would bring approved construction debt past $1.4 billion in ten years while test scores lag; it questions $161.3 million for a Chinook partial remodel not starting until 2031 and asks voters to 'Vote No for Now' for a smaller bond.

taxes.basis: A yes vote authorizes $595.4 million in new bonds, on top of the 2016 (~$299M) and 2022 ($518.4M) bonds; the district's table shows total bond rates (existing plus proposed) of $2.30 per $1,000 in 2026 and $2.36 to $2.25 in 2027-2030. The con case centers on debt size.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1) and statements (S2); Resolution 11-26 (S3); district bond, cost, FAQ, CFAC and per-project pages (S4-S17); district 2022 bond pages (S18-S19); B-Town Blog coverage (S20-S23); Yes for Highline and Better Plan for Highline committee sites (S24-S27); Board Policy 6101 (S28); PDC records for Yes For Highline (S29-S30).

measures.what_it_does: Approves a four-year Highline capital levy of $12 million a year (2027-2030) for districtwide technology (cybersecurity, internet, devices, software, staff training and support) and some building-system capital improvements. It resumes local technology levy funding that lapsed after the two-year 2020 levy (collected 2021-2022).
measures.cost_line: Estimated $0.36 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027, $0.35 in 2028, $0.34 in 2029 and $0.32 in 2030 ($12,000,000 each year, $48 million total). The district's combined estimate for Props. 1 and 2 is about $210 a year more on a $500,000 home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Trisha Arias, Karen Keiser, Pat Thompson, www.yesforHighline.org) says the levy restores expired voter-approved funding for cybersecurity, reliable internet, devices, software, teacher training and parent communication systems that state funding does not cover, and is 'not more screentime.'
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Mike Bishoff, Katie Paulson, Lauren Schmidt, BetterPlanforHighline.com) says students need human-led instruction rather than more tech contracts, objects to 1:1 devices from kindergarten and to i-Ready, and calls the levy a 'blank check' under the June 2026 revision of Policy 6101; it asks for contract audits, early-grade device removal, screen policies and stronger board oversight.

taxes.basis: A yes vote restores a lapsed technology levy at $0.32-$0.36 per $1,000, about half the 2020 levy's 67-cent rate. It is a new line on current tax bills after a four-year gap, but a modest one.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1) and statements (S2); Resolution 12-26 (S3); district bond-and-levy, tech levy, FAQ and cost pages (S4-S7); B-Town Blog coverage of the 2020 tech levy and 2025 education levy (S8, S9, S11); district 2025 levy page (S10); Board Policy 6101 and Procedure 6101 P3 (S12-S13); Better Plan for Highline and Yes for Highline committee sites (S14-S17); PDC records for Yes For Highline (S18-S19).

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Kent School District's educational programs and operations levy, which expires at the end of 2027, with a four-year levy for 2028-2031. The levy funds staff, programs and operating costs the state does not cover, about 15% of the district's general operating budget.
measures.cost_line: Approximately $1.95 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2028 ($104.7 million), $1.93 in 2029 ($111.1 million), $1.88 in 2030 ($115.7 million) and $1.84 in 2031 ($121.4 million). The expiring levy was estimated at about $1.72 per $1,000 ($85.8 million in its last year) when voters approved it in 2023.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Dana Ralph, Bill Boyce, Jeff Wagner, citizensforkentschools.com) says this renewal is 'not a new tax' and keeps funding safety, academic support, athletics, arts, mental health and transportation while keeping one of the lowest levy rates among neighboring districts; it cites seven consecutive clean financial audits.
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Joseph Riley) says the district wants significantly more money while cutting programs and staff, offers no binding promises, and is running the levy a year early, so a 'No' costs classrooms nothing in 2027 and the district can return with a community-aligned plan.

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews an expiring EP&O levy at a moderately higher rate and amount than its 2023 estimates ($1.95 vs about $1.72 per $1,000; $104.7M vs $85.8M), not a doubling, so it is treated as a replacement levy.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1) and statements (S2); Kent Reporter coverage of the 2026 levy, the board vote, the timing, budget cuts and the 2023 levy (S3-S11); RCW 84.52.0531 (S12); Citizens for Kent Schools site (S13); PDC records for Citizens for Kent Schools (S14-S15). The Kent district website could not be retrieved (bot challenge).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes Fire District 20 (Skyway/West Hill) to issue up to $16 million in 20-year bonds. The money would renovate its fire station, replace and redevelop two support sites with secure storage, parking and backup power, and buy fire apparatus.
measures.cost_line: Up to $16,000,000 in bonds repaid by an excess property tax estimated at about $0.28 per $1,000 of assessed value. The district estimates $196 a year ($16.33 a month) on a $700,000 home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Terry Miller, Alesia D. Cannday, Margie Lindberg) says the bond would modernize a station 'built more than 40 years ago and is not seismic approved', replace an aging reserve engine, and build secure storage. It says these capital needs cannot be met from the district's operating budget.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed. No one volunteered for the opposition committee.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a new bond-repayment excess levy of about $0.28 per $1,000. The district has no bond levy now; its 2026 total rate is $1.50.

measures.sources_note: Sources: pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); statement in favor (S2); Resolution 2026-002 (S3); the district's bond page, community presentation and district pages (S4-S7); King County Assessor levy tables for 2015, 2020, 2025 and 2026 (S8-S11); PDC query showing no committees (S12). No news coverage was found.

measures.what_it_does: Permanently raises the Vashon-Maury Island cemetery district's property tax levy. The money would cover operating costs, modernize burial records, buy equipment, develop green burial, and help buy more land.
measures.cost_line: Raises the levy from approximately $.03 ($.02816) to $.05 per $1,000 of assessed value beginning in 2027. The district says this is about $2 more per $100,000 of assessed value; the Beachcomber estimates about $17 more a year for a median island home.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The district's resolution says tax revenue has fallen short of expenses every year since 2021, with plot sales covering the gap.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed. No one volunteered for either committee.

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a permanent levy lid lift on an existing levy, from $0.02816 to $0.05 per $1,000 (about 78% higher). The dollar amount is very small: about $2 per $100,000 of assessed value. Scored 1 instead of 2 because it raises an existing small levy rather than creating a new tax; the lead may prefer 2 given the relative size of the increase.

spending.basis: The ballot title names expansion purposes beyond current operations: developing green burial practices, acquiring more property, a truck, and modernized records.

measures.sources_note: Sources: pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); no statements filed (S2); Resolution 295 (S3); district website and 2024 annual report (S4-S6); Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber coverage from 2026 and 2023 (S7, S8); King County Assessor levy tables for 2025 and 2026 (S9, S10); PDC query showing no committees (S11).

measures.what_it_does: Adds a county charter section requiring the County Council to adopt and maintain a Foundational Government Services Policy that prioritizes funding for state-mandated offices (Assessor, Auditor, Clerk, Executive, Prosecuting Attorney, Sheriff, Treasurer, District and Superior Court judges) and foundational services before the expansion of discretionary programs, and promotes balanced budgets and reserves.
measures.cost_line: No tax, rate or dollar amount; it sets a budget priority and does not appropriate money or fix funding levels.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Brian Sullivan) says it puts essential services first, ahead of discretionary programs, and promotes balanced budgets and reserves without raising taxes or dictating spending levels.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Christine Eck and Janice Green) says the named offices are already legally required, 'foundational' is undefined, and the vague mandate invites litigation and weakens the Council's open budget authority.

spending.basis: YES writes into the charter a priority for funding state-mandated foundational services 'before the expansion of discretionary programs,' plus structural budget balance and reserves: a restraint-before-expansion principle, though it sets no spending level.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); statements for and against with rebuttals (S2); Charter Review Commission amendment text, new Section 6.140 (S3); Everett Herald, June 24, 2026 (S4); PDC committee search, none found (S5).

measures.what_it_does: Adds a county charter section requiring a Primary Stabilization Fund and a separate Secondary Catastrophic Stabilization Fund (run by the Treasurer, seeded with 10% of the primary fund), funded from investment earnings, one-time revenues and emergency reimbursements; spending from either fund needs four of five council votes, and catastrophic-fund withdrawals need a replenishment plan.
measures.cost_line: No new tax; the catastrophic fund may not be funded by taxes or fees imposed solely for it. Existing revenue streams are redirected into reserves.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Brian Sullivan) says it builds emergency savings before the next crisis, limits reserves to genuine emergencies, and cites the $22 million the county spent from its General Fund in six weeks after the Oso slide.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Hans Dunshee and Janice R. Greene) calls it unnecessary and rigid, says a county fund is too small for a true disaster and diverts money from services, and objects that a four-of-five vote lets a council minority block spending.

spending.basis: YES channels existing revenue into reserves and requires a four-of-five council supermajority, with replenishment plans, before money in either stabilization fund can be spent: saving and restraint over current spending.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); statements for and against with rebuttals (S2); amendment text, new Section 6.150 (S3); Everett Herald, June 24, 2026 (S4); PDC committee search, none found (S5).

measures.what_it_does: Makes every Snohomish County elected office nonpartisan, removing party preference from the ballot for the County Council and Executive (from 2027 and 2029 by district) and Prosecuting Attorney (from 2030), and ends the rule that partisan vacancies are filled from names submitted by the departing official's party.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate; changes how county offices appear on the ballot.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Todd Welch, Mark James and Shawn O'Donnell) says county services are not partisan, the change matches the county's other elected offices and every city, and it widens the pool of candidates.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Anna Maria Jackson Laurence, Janice R. Greene and James Kenny) says party labels give voters useful information chosen under I-872, and removing them hides party influence rather than ending it.
measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); statements for and against (S2); amendment text, Sections 4.15, 4.80 and transitional 11.090-11.140 (S3); Everett Herald (S4); PDC (S5). No rubric measure axis covers ballot party labels.

measures.what_it_does: Adds a county charter section requiring free, searchable and downloadable public financial data (spending, contracts, grants, recipients, budget lines, audits) built from information the county already collects, 'where reasonably practicable' and phased in as systems are modernized.
measures.cost_line: No tax or appropriation in the measure; opponents cite budget-office testimony that adding a public portal to the current $15 million financial-system overhaul would be costly.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Danny Perkins and Janelle M. Cass) says residents should see how public dollars are spent without records requests, and a charter commitment keeps transparency built into future systems.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Doris Fulton and Janice R. Greene) supports the goal but says 'reasonably practicable' has no force and a funded ordinance would deliver a real portal.
measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); statements for and against (S2); amendment text, new Section 6.130 (S3); Everett Herald (S4); PDC (S5). Oversight theme only; no confident spending direction.

measures.what_it_does: Amends charter Section 2.20 so that, after January 1, 2027, any new councilmanic tax (one the council can levy without a public vote but has not yet levied, or gains authority for later) may be assessed, levied or increased only by four of five councilmembers. Existing taxes and same-rate renewals, fees, rates, charges and special assessments are exempt.
measures.cost_line: No tax change; raises the council vote needed for new non-voted county taxes from a majority to four of five.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Todd Welch, Dan Perkins and Janelle Cass) says it requires broad council agreement before taxing residents more without a vote, protecting fixed-income seniors, young families and small businesses, without cutting services.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Paula Rhyne, John Lovick and Mike Sells) says it gives two of five councilmembers a veto over the majority and could block routine levies for deputies, courts, roads and veterans services.

taxes.basis: YES adds a four-of-five supermajority requirement before the council can impose or increase new non-voted county taxes, a structural limit on raising taxes (pole A). Existing taxes and same-rate renewals are exempt.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); statements for and against with rebuttals (S2); amendment text, Section 2.20 with the 'new councilmanic tax' definition and exemptions (S3); Everett Herald (S4); PDC (S5).

measures.what_it_does: Annexes the City of Bothell (Snohomish and King County voters in Bothell vote on the same question) into the Shoreline Fire Department Regional Fire Authority on March 1, 2027. The Bothell Fire Department becomes part of the RFA, whose nine-member board would include three Bothell City Councilmembers.
measures.cost_line: The ballot title gives no rate. From 2028 the RFA levy and fire benefit charge would apply to Bothell property; the city says it intends to cut its own general levy, but no net figure is published.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Wesley Wang, Brandon Keith and Mason Thompson) says regional fire service is the standard model, shares resources and future facility costs across a larger tax base, and keeps Bothell three of nine board seats; IAFF Local 2099 endorses it.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed, and the city reports no applicants for the con committee.

local-control.basis: YES moves fire and EMS governance from the Bothell City Council to a nine-member regional fire authority board on which Bothell appoints three seats.

taxes.basis: YES places the RFA's own property-tax levy and fire benefit charge on Bothell property from 2028; the city's intended offsetting cut to its general levy is not part of the measure and no net figure is published.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title, explanatory statement and statement for, with no statement against (S1); Shoreline Fire RFA FAQ on Bothell and Sno10 (S2); City of Bothell Fire Service Study page (S3).

measures.what_it_does: Requires Everett Mayor and Council candidates to have been registered city voters and city (or district) residents for one year before the filing deadline, bars the Mayor and councilmembers from holding any other elected office at the same time (the Everett seat is vacated), and limits the oath requirement to elected officials.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate; amends the city charter.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Todd Welch, Randy Bolerjack and Jonathan Peebles) says one office at a time and a year of residency keep representatives focused on and rooted in Everett, while unhoused residents can still run.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; no one contacted the Auditor's office to write one.
measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title, explanatory statement and statement for, no con (S1); Ordinance No. 4189-26 charter text (S2); Everett Herald, July 17, 2026 (S3); PDC, none found (S4). No rubric measure axis applies.

measures.what_it_does: Lowers the Everett City Council's minimum regular meetings from 48 to 36 a year, with at least two a month and a schedule published each January, and has the Vice-President (or a councilmember the President designates) preside when the President is absent.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate; amends the city charter.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Alan Rubio, Alice Hedges and Marcus Nuñez) says the decades-old 48-meeting rule produces thin agendas held to meet a count, and 36 gives flexibility with predictable meetings.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; no one contacted the Auditor's office to write one.
measures.sources_note: Pamphlet (S1); Ordinance No. 4189-26 Section 3.2 text (S2); Everett Herald (S3); PDC (S4). Internal governance; no rubric measure axis applies.

measures.what_it_does: Narrows the Everett Civil Service Commission's charter role from classifying and running eligibility-list hiring for most city employees to the hiring examination processes state law requires for police officers and firefighters (chapters 41.08 and 41.12 RCW); other hiring follows state law and union contracts.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate; amends the city charter.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Randy Bolerjack and Brent Terry) says eligibility lists up to three years old force hiring from stale applicant pools, and applying for specific openings would modernize hiring.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; no one contacted the Auditor's office to write one.
measures.sources_note: Pamphlet (S1); Ordinance No. 4189-26 Section 8.3 text and explanatory statement (S2); Everett Herald (S3); PDC (S4). Personnel administration; no rubric measure axis applies.

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Everett's two initiative thresholds (15% of the last general municipal election to force council action or a special election; 5% to reach the next regular election) with one 10% threshold based on the last Mayoral election, keeps referenda at 10% on the same Mayoral base, adds sponsor committees and a 10-day signature cure period, and requires a Finance Director fiscal impact statement for qualifying initiatives.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate; adds a fiscal impact statement for qualifying initiatives.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Mason Rutledge and Brent Terry) says a single signature standard, clearer petition procedures and fiscal impact statements give clearer rules and better-informed voters.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; no one contacted the Auditor's office to write one.
measures.sources_note: Pamphlet (S1); Ordinance No. 4189-26 Sections 11.1-11.5 current and amended text (S2); Everett Herald, whose threshold description differs from the charter text (S3); PDC (S4). Direct-democracy procedure; the rubric's reform axis does not apply to measures.

measures.what_it_does: Lets Everett publish legal notices, appointments, ordinance summaries, proposed initiatives and referenda, bid advertisements, franchises and proposed charter amendments on the city website as an alternative to the official newspaper, with copies available at the City Clerk's office.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate; supporters say it reduces print costs (no estimate given).
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Alice Hedges, Mason Rutledge and Todd Welch) says the print-era charter should let notices go online, where they are available around the clock, expanding rather than shrinking transparency.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; no one contacted the Auditor's office to write one.
measures.sources_note: Pamphlet (S1); Ordinance No. 4189-26 amended sections adding 'or on the City's website' (S2); Everett Herald (S3); PDC (S4). Administrative; no rubric measure axis applies.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes a four-year capital projects levy (2027-2030) for school safety and security upgrades, major maintenance (roofs, HVAC, fire and security systems) and relocating Sky Valley Education Center to the updated Wagner Center site.
measures.cost_line: $12,282,731 a year for 2027-2030, an estimated $0.95 to $0.82 per $1,000 of assessed value (district average 88 cents).
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Kyle Fisher and Molly Barnes) says the district listened after February's bond failed, cutting the request from about $152 million over 20 years to $49 million over four years for urgent safety and repair needs.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed.

taxes.basis: YES adds a new four-year excess property-tax levy of about $12.3 million a year (about $0.82-$0.95 per $1,000).

spending.basis: YES funds a focused capital program of maintenance and safety work, smaller and shorter than the bond voters rejected in February.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title, explanatory statement and statement for (S1); Everett Herald, June 17 2026, levy contents, February 48.9% bond result and average rate (S2).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes $400 million in 21-year bonds to replace parts of Mukilteo, Serene Lake and Olivia Park elementaries and Explorer Middle School, expand the Kamiak gym, rebuild athletic facilities, and upgrade technology, safety and building systems. Voters gave the same bond 57.2% in February, short of 60%.
measures.cost_line: Average excess levy of $0.57 per $1,000 over the bonds' life; the district estimates an increase of about 20 cents per $1,000, about $132 a year for the median home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Judith M. Schwab, Nhi Pham and Angela Gottula) says many schools predate the Vietnam War, recent emergency repairs show failing infrastructure, and the bond unlocks about $30 million in state match.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Howard Damoff) says the same bond failed in February, enrollment is down, debt and interest are already high, and interest-free capital levies would be cheaper.

taxes.basis: YES adds 21 years of bond excess levies averaging $0.57 per $1,000, an estimated increase of about $132 a year for the median home.

spending.basis: YES funds a $400 million capital program including four school replacements; opponents call it too much and propose smaller pay-as-you-go levies.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); statements for and against with rebuttals (S2); Everett Herald, July 22 2026, February 57.2% result and cost per home (S3).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes $160 million in 21-year bonds to modernize Gold Bar Elementary (pre-K to 2), Sultan Middle (grades 3-5) and Sultan High (grades 6-8) sites, build a new high school (9-12) with expanded career and technical education, and repurpose Sultan Elementary.
measures.cost_line: $160 million in bonds over up to 21 years, repaid by excess property taxes; the pamphlet gives no rate.
measures.pro_summary: No statement for was filed. The district's explanatory statement says the bonds improve safety, reduce portable classrooms and move the youngest students out of the floodplain.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed.

taxes.basis: YES adds 21 years of excess property taxes to repay $160 million in bonds; no rate is stated.

spending.basis: YES funds a large capital program including a new high school and three school modernizations.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement, with no statements for or against (S1); Everett Herald, Nov 5 2024, election-night result of the district's previous $79 million bond (46.9%) (S2).

measures.what_it_does: Annexes Snohomish County Fire Protection District No. 10 (unincorporated area around Bothell, now served by contract with Bothell) into the Shoreline Fire Department Regional Fire Authority on March 1, 2027. The district would dissolve at the end of 2027 and its residents get no seats on the RFA board.
measures.cost_line: The RFA levy (estimated $0.45 per $1,000 from 2028) replaces the district's levy (about $0.90), plus a fire benefit charge set in 2028; the RFA's preliminary estimate is a net saving of about $0.20 per $1,000.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Morris Parrish, Jack Barnes and Craig Bishop) says the Bothell-area fire service has not grown with population and a regional authority brings shared resources, training and permanent, reliable funding; the Bothell firefighters' union endorses it.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed.

local-control.basis: YES dissolves the district's own elected board and moves governance to a regional board on which district residents get no seats.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title, explanatory statement and statement for (S1); Shoreline Fire RFA FAQ on Bothell and Sno10, including the Sno10 dissolution and preliminary tax estimate (S2). No taxes lean: the pamphlet describes a levy swap plus a benefit charge whose net effect is only a preliminary estimate.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes South County Fire to issue up to $420 million in bonds over up to 25 years to replace six stations, build four new ones, seismically upgrade four, and build or improve support facilities, repaid by excess property taxes.
measures.cost_line: Levies expected to average about $0.194 per $1,000 of assessed value; the Herald reports about $136 a year for a $700,000 home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Shannon Sessions, Alex Johnson and Steve Barnes) cites an assessment that two-thirds of stations need major work and nearly half could fail in a major earthquake, and a 30% rise in calls over a decade.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Melinda Goforth, Mary Jane Goss and Jim Landers) says the bond exceeds half a billion dollars with interest during an affordability crisis and asks the district to fund only the six high-risk station replacements ($136.7 million).

taxes.basis: YES adds a new excess property-tax levy averaging about $0.194 per $1,000 (about $136 a year for a $700,000 home) for up to 25 years.

spending.basis: YES funds a $420 million capital program of replacements, renovations, four new stations and support facilities; opponents ask to fund only the top-priority replacements.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title and explanatory statement (S1); statements for and against with rebuttals (S2); Everett Herald, Oct 3 2026, station list, seismic assessment and cost per home (S3); Everett Herald, June 10 2026, board action and Edmonds mayor's request to reduce the bond (S4).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes Public Hospital District No. 1 (EvergreenHealth Monroe) to issue up to $382 million in 30-year bonds to build and equip a replacement hospital on its Monroe campus. The same bond had 55.6% one week into the August primary count, short of the 60% required.
measures.cost_line: Estimated average $0.437 per $1,000, about $40.75 a month for a $745,000 home (about $489 a year for a median home).
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Dianne Forth, Michael Eickerman and Ernie Walters) says the hospital is aging and overcrowded, and a replacement adds capacity and technology and keeps care local, with audits and local oversight.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed.

taxes.basis: YES adds a 30-year excess property-tax levy averaging $0.437 per $1,000 to repay up to $382 million in bonds.

spending.basis: YES funds a large public capital investment in a replacement hospital with added beds, emergency and surgical capacity.

measures.sources_note: Pamphlet ballot title, explanatory statement and statement for (S1); Everett Herald, May 4 2026, project scope and cost per home (S2); Everett Herald, August 2026 primary results for the same bond (S3).

measures.what_it_does: Creates a new 0.1% city sales and use tax for police, public safety and criminal justice services in Liberty Lake (RCW 82.14.450). It has no stated end date, and the city keeps 85% of the money; 15% goes to Spokane County.
measures.cost_line: Adds 10 cents to a $100 taxable purchase, raising Liberty Lake's sales tax from 9.0% to 9.1%. The city projects about $750,000 a year.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (For committee contact Kathryn Lynn Atkins) says public safety must grow with the city, costs have risen sharply in four years, and the general fund alone is not a sustainable source. It says visitors and shoppers would share the cost, not just homeowners.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote creates a new 0.1% sales tax with no stated end date, raising the combined rate from 9.0% to 9.1% and about $750,000 a year.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7351 (S1); the city's Proposition 1 Q&A page (S2); Spokesman-Review coverage of the measure and the 6-0 council vote (S3); DOR Q4 2026 rates (S4); RCW 82.14.450 (S5); Spokesman-Review on the 2025 state public safety sales tax law (S6); PDC query showing no committee (S7).

measures.what_it_does: Renews Rockford's one-year property tax levy for town fire protection in 2027. It replaces the expiring levy at the same rate the town has used in recent years.
measures.cost_line: About $0.51 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027, raising $40,934.57 (about $153 on a $300,000 home). The 2026 levy was $0.51, raising $36,075.08.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The town says the levy is needed to maintain fire service, staffing, equipment and facilities as costs rise.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews a recurring one-year fire levy at the same $0.51 rate approved for 2025 and 2026. It is a replacement, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7352 (S1); Rockford council minutes from July 15, 2026 (S2) and July 5, 2023 (S5); VoteWA records for the 2025 and 2026 fire levies (S3, S4); Secretary of State results for 2023-2025 (S6-S8). No news coverage was found.

measures.what_it_does: Renews Spangle's one-year excess property tax levy that pays the town's fire protection contract with Spokane County Fire District 3 in 2027.
measures.cost_line: About $1.40 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027, raising $49,000 (about $420 on a $300,000 home). This is the same rate and amount as the 2025 and 2026 levies.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The town says no other funds, grants or loans are available to pay its Fire District 3 contract.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews Spangle's recurring one-year fire levy at the same $1.40 rate and $49,000 amount as the last two years. It is a replacement, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7353 (S1); VoteWA records for the 2024-2026 fire levies (S2-S4); Secretary of State results for 2024 and 2025 (S5, S6); the town's July 13, 2026 meeting agenda (S7); Fire District 3's EMS levy FAQ (S8). No news coverage was found.

measures.what_it_does: Renews Spangle's one-year excess property tax levy that pays the town's police protection contract with the Spokane County Sheriff's Office in 2027.
measures.cost_line: About $1.19 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027, raising $28,000 (about $357 on a $300,000 home). This is the same rate and amount as the 2026 levy.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The town says no other grants or loans are available to pay its sheriff's contract.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews Spangle's recurring one-year police levy at the same $1.19 rate and $28,000 amount as this year. It is a replacement, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7354 (S1); VoteWA records for the 2024-2026 police levies (S2-S4); Secretary of State results for 2024 and 2025 (S5, S6); the town's July 13, 2026 meeting agenda (S7). No news coverage was found.

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Central Valley School District's educational programs and operations levy, which expires at the end of 2027, with a three-year levy for 2028-2030. It pays for staff, nurses, counselors, safety staff, music, athletics, advanced courses and activities the state does not fully fund, about 16% of district revenue.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $2.50 per $1,000 of assessed value each year, the same rate collected in 2026: $48.9 million in 2028, $50.55 million in 2029 and $52.4 million in 2030. The district estimates about $1,045 a year on a $418,000 median home. The expiring levy authorized $137 million over 2025-2027.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Central Valley Citizens for Education: Lindsay Miller, Cris Kaminskas, Buffy Nustad; YesCVSchools.org) says 'Replace the levy. Keep the rate.' It says the levy funds advanced and technical courses, arts, athletics, nurses, counselors and safety staff, and will not exceed the current $2.50 rate.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was received (the listed committee is Dennis Reed). In news coverage, board Vice President Anniece Barker voted to send the levy to the ballot but said 'I do not support continuing to raise taxes on our community,' citing the roughly 3.5% yearly increases in the levy amount. The Spokane County Republican Party chair said the party has resolved to support no new taxes for five years and that districts should 'lean it up.'

taxes.basis: A yes vote continues an expiring EP&O levy at the same $2.50 per $1,000 rate collected in 2026, with dollar amounts about 3.5% higher each year. This is a replacement levy at the same rate, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7350 (S1); CVSD levy page (S2); Central Valley Citizens for Education site (S3); Spokesman-Review coverage of the 2026 board vote and campaign (S4-S5), the 2024 levy (S6) and February 2024 results (S7).

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Cheney School District's educational programs and operation levy, which expires in 2027, with a three-year levy for 2028-2030. It pays for athletics, activities, counselors, nurses, paraeducators, smaller classes, special education, safety and other costs the state does not fund.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $2.10 per $1,000 of assessed value each year: $18.45 million in 2028, $19 million in 2029 and $19.55 million in 2030, about $57 million in total. The expiring levy was estimated at $1.97 per $1,000 (about $51 million over three years) when the board sent it to the February 2024 ballot.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Committee for Great Schools: Meridth Lemelin, Nicole Williams, Amy Pruett) says the levy maintains current programs, failure would bring 'drastic cuts,' and 'This is not a new tax.'
measures.con_summary: No statement against was submitted; the voters' guide says no volunteers came forward after repeated recruitment attempts.

taxes.basis: A yes vote replaces an expiring EP&O levy that is moderately larger than before: about $57 million versus about $51 million, and an estimated $2.10 versus $1.97 per $1,000. The district projects the combined school rate to fall from $3.93 to $3.90. This is a replacement levy, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7328 (S1); Cheney Public Schools levy page (S2); Spokesman-Review coverage of the 2026 levies (S3-S4), the 2024 levy (S5) and February 2024 results (S6).

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Cheney School District's capital levy, which expires in 2027, with a three-year levy for 2028-2030. It pays for instructional technology, security cameras and entry controls, and safety infrastructure such as roofing, HVAC, plumbing, lighting and fencing.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $0.10 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2028 ($880,000), $0.15 in 2029 ($1.35 million) and $0.20 in 2030 ($1.9 million), about $4.1 million in total. The expiring capital levy was estimated at 9 cents per $1,000 (about $2.3 million over three years) when it went to voters in 2024.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Committee for Great Schools: Meridth Lemelin, Nicole Williams, Amy Pruett) calls it 'a replacement levy, not a new tax.' It says the levy funds classroom technology, roof, HVAC and fire-alarm work, and security cameras and door locks, and that deferring maintenance would cost more later.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was submitted; the voters' guide says no volunteers came forward after repeated recruitment attempts.

taxes.basis: A yes vote replaces an expiring capital levy. The new levy is larger than the expiring levy's 2024 estimate (about $4.1 million at 10-20 cents versus $2.3 million at 9 cents), but the district projects the combined school rate to dip from $3.93 to $3.90. Scored as a replacement. The rise in this levy alone is a case for +2.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7329 (S1); Cheney Public Schools levy page (S2); Spokesman-Review coverage of the 2026 levies (S3-S4), the 2024 levies (S5) and February 2024 results (S6).

measures.what_it_does: Replaces East Valley School District's capital levy, which expires at the end of 2026, with a two-year levy for 2027-2028. It pays for safety, security and communication systems, parking and traffic work, plumbing, HVAC, roof and electrical replacement, and technology. It follows two failed 2026 bonds to replace the high school and middle school.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $0.99 per $1,000 of assessed value: $6,793,300 in 2027 and $6,996,996 in 2028, about $446 a year on a $450,000 property. Reporting earlier in 2026 said an existing 74-cent school levy was set to expire.
measures.pro_summary: No statement for was submitted. In news coverage, Superintendent Mandi Rehn said aging buildings need roof and HVAC work and the levy would keep them functional after the bond failed twice.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was submitted. In news coverage, the Spokane County Republican Party chair said the party opposes any new taxes for five years, while sympathizing with the district's needs.

taxes.basis: The ballot title describes a replacement of an expiring capital levy. The estimated rate of $0.99 is about 25 cents above the 74-cent levy reported as expiring, similar to other replacement levies with moderate increases. Scored as a replacement, not a new tax. One Spokesman-Review article says the earlier capital levy expired in 2022, which leaves what is being replaced uncertain.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7355 (S1); Spokesman-Review coverage of the levy (S2) and the failed 2026 bonds (S3-S5). The East Valley district website returned a bot challenge.

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Nine Mile Falls School District's educational programs and operations levy, which expires in 2027, with a three-year levy for 2028-2030. It pays for staff, class size reduction, nurses, counselors, music and arts, athletics and activities, transportation and other costs the state does not fund, about 17% of the budget.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $2.10 per $1,000 of assessed value each year: $4,354,837 in 2028, $4,428,827 in 2029 and $4,504,075 in 2030. The current levy collects $2.27 per $1,000 in 2026.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was received by the deadline (the listed committee is Supporting Nine Mile Students, Ann Fackenthall). In news coverage, Superintendent Jeff Baerwald called the levy the district's 'lifeblood' and said the district is lowering the rate.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (NO Means NO! Voters Said NO Just 90 Days Ago!, David Joplin) says voters rejected a district levy 90 days earlier. It argues this levy lets the district spend on anything 'not funded by the State,' and says the district ranks 50th in income but 235th in dollars per student.

taxes.basis: A yes vote replaces an expiring EP&O levy at a lower estimated rate, $2.10 versus the $2.27 collected in 2026. This is a replacement levy, not a new or larger tax.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7330 (S1); Spokesman-Review coverage of the November levies (S2), February 2024 results (S3) and the failed April 2026 capital levy (S4). The district website returned a bot challenge.

measures.what_it_does: A new six-year capital levy (2027-2032) to replace the failing roof and condemned portable classrooms at Lakeside High School and update fire alarm, security camera and other systems. A larger capital levy failed in April 2026.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $0.38 per $1,000 of assessed value each year, from $774,853 in 2027 rising to $842,954 in 2032 (about $4.85 million in total). That equals the rate of a 20-year construction bond that is paid off at the end of 2026, so the district's rate would not rise.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Future Focused For Nine Mile: Melanie Reynolds, Devin Bauer, Candace Haggard) says the levy keeps the current tax rate by replacing an expiring bond at the same 38 cents. It says the board cut projects after hearing tax concerns, and the levy funds a failed roof, condemned classrooms and required fire and camera systems.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (NO Means NO! Voters Said NO Just 90 Days Ago!, David Joplin) says voters rejected a capital levy 90 days earlier. It calls this version vague 'carte blanche' spending, says the district recovers its election costs through it, and argues the portables are not essential.

taxes.basis: Legally a new levy, but it continues the 38-cent rate of a construction bond that expires at the end of 2026. A yes vote holds the district's rate in place and a no vote lowers it, the same effect as a same-rate replacement. The district projects a combined rate of $2.48 in 2028 versus $2.65 in 2026. Treating it as a 'new tax' would argue for +2.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7331 (S1); Spokesman-Review coverage of the November levies (S2) and the April 2026 capital levy and its failure (S3-S4).

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Riverside School District's educational programs and operations levy, which expires at the end of 2027, with a three-year levy for 2028-2030. It pays for electives and advanced courses, vocational education, nurses, counselors, technology support, safety, performing arts, athletics and activities, about 13% of the budget.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $1.58 per $1,000 of assessed value each year: $3,996,811 in 2028, $4,116,715 in 2029 and $4,240,217 in 2030. Taxpayers currently pay $1.52 per $1,000 for the expiring levy.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Community for the Riverside Replacement Levy: Jeni Vineyard, Kevin Koesel, Jennifer Gaffaney) says the levy replaces the current one rather than adding a second. It says the levy funds courses, nurses, counselors, safety, arts and athletics that are 'not extras' to students.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was submitted; the voters' guide says no volunteers came forward after repeated recruitment attempts. Voters rejected a separate Riverside capital levy in November 2025.

taxes.basis: A yes vote replaces the expiring EP&O levy at a similar rate, an estimated $1.58 versus $1.52 per $1,000 now. This is a replacement levy, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7332 (S1); Spokesman-Review coverage of the levy (S2), the failed 2025 capital levy (S3) and February 2024 results (S4). District levy materials were not found on the district website.

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Spokane Public Schools' educational programs and operation levy, which expires at the end of 2027, with a three-year levy for 2028-2030. It pays for class size, advanced courses, special education, nurses, counselors, safety staff, music, athletics and activities the state does not fully fund, about 15% of the operating budget.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $2.50 per $1,000 of assessed value, the same rate as the current levy: $107 million in 2028, $111 million in 2029 and $115 million in 2030 ($333 million in total). The county assessor puts it at about $830 a year on the district's $333,700 average home. The expiring levy authorized $297 million over three years.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Carol Wendle) cites clean financial audits, more than 200 positions cut to balance the budget, and gains in early literacy, graduation and career pathways. Its rebuttal says failure would mean cutting another 700 positions.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Russell Neff) says the levy takes the legal maximum rate for three years from stretched families. It says about 97% funds extra salaries the state should pay, and that test scores and absenteeism do not justify it. It says students will still be educated if it fails.

taxes.basis: A yes vote replaces the expiring EP&O levy at the same $2.50 per $1,000 rate, with dollar amounts about 12% higher than the 2024 levy ($333 million versus $297 million over three years). This is a replacement levy at the same rate, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7356 (S1); Spokesman-Review coverage of the 2026 levy (S2-S5) and the 2024 levy and bond (S6-S7). The district levy webpage returned a bot challenge.

measures.what_it_does: Replaces West Valley School District's educational programs and operations levy, which expires at the end of 2027, with a three-year levy for 2028-2030. It pays for smaller classes, advanced courses, nurses, counselors, technology, safety, music, athletics, activities and facility maintenance, about 15% of the budget.
