measures.cost_line: Estimated $2.50 per $1,000 of assessed value each year, the same as 2026 collections: $10,479,522 in 2028, $10,793,908 in 2029 and $10,955,816 in 2030 (about $32.2 million). The district projects $1,308 a year for a $375,000 home for this levy and Proposition 2 combined.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (EP&O Replacement 'For' Levy Committee: Eric Rosentrater, Jodee Cahalan) says 'This is not a new tax.' It says the levy funds smaller classes, advanced courses, nurses, counselors, technology, safety, music and athletics without increasing the tax rate.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was submitted; the voters' guide says no volunteers came forward after repeated recruitment attempts.

taxes.basis: A yes vote replaces the expiring EP&O levy at the same $2.50 rate collected in 2026, with a modestly larger amount: $32.2 million versus the $30 million sent to voters for 2025-2027. This is a replacement levy, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7357 (S1); West Valley levy page and election notice (S2-S3); Spokesman-Review coverage of the 2026 levies (S4-S5), the 2024 levy (S6) and February 2024 results (S7).

measures.what_it_does: Replaces West Valley School District's capital levy, which expires at the end of 2027, with a two-year levy for 2028-2029. It pays for entrance security (cameras, access controls, door locks), HVAC replacement at Spokane Valley High, a library addition at Pasadena Park Elementary, and sprinkler and abatement work.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $1.00 per $1,000 of assessed value: $4,191,809 in 2028 and $4,317,563 in 2029, about $8.5 million. The district projects the combined rate of both November levies at $3.50 per $1,000, compared with $3.49 in 2026.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Capital Projects Levy 'For' Committee: Eric Rosentrater, Jodee Cahalan) says the levy focuses on school entrance security and replacing Spokane Valley High's outdated HVAC, plus fire sprinkler and abatement work. It calls the levy 'responsible' and 'time-limited.'
measures.con_summary: No statement against was submitted; the voters' guide says no volunteers came forward after repeated recruitment attempts.

taxes.basis: A yes vote replaces an expiring capital levy approved in 2024. The district projects the combined rate of both levies to be essentially unchanged ($3.50 versus $3.49 per $1,000). This is a replacement at about the same rate, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7358 (S1); West Valley levy page and election notice (S2-S3); Spokesman-Review coverage of the 2026 levies (S4-S5).

measures.what_it_does: Renews Fire District 2's six-year emergency medical services property tax levy for the Fairfield and Mount Hope area. The money pays for the district's volunteer EMS and ambulance service.
measures.cost_line: $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed value a year, collected 2027 through 2032 ($150 a year on a $300,000 home). This is the same rate as the expiring levy approved in 2020.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Renew EMS Levy committee: Steven Braun, David DeGon, Stephen Primmer, Connie Reinhardt) says this continues the current levy, not a new tax. It says the money is dedicated to EMS and keeps local ambulance operations, personnel and medical equipment going.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews an expiring six-year EMS levy at the same $0.50 rate the district collects now. It is a replacement, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7359 (S1); Spokesman-Review interview with Chief Eric Olson (S2); the 2020 EMS levy record and result (S3, S4); RCW 84.52.069 (S5).

measures.what_it_does: Creates a new six-year emergency medical services property tax levy for Fire District 3 (Cheney, Medical Lake, Four Lakes, Spangle area). The district says it would fund 14 firefighter/EMTs and add 24-hour staffing at stations in Cheney and Spangle.
measures.cost_line: Up to $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed value a year for six years starting in 2027: $50 a year per $100,000 ($250 on a $500,000 home), about $2.79 million a year. The district's combined rate would go from $1.48 to about $1.98.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (committee contact Dale Fulfs) says rising costs have already left two positions unfilled. It says the levy would staff two more stations around the clock, improve response times across the district, and that the district has managed money responsibly.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a new EMS levy of up to $0.50 per $1,000 on top of the $1.48 fire levy, which the district itself calls a new levy. A similar EMS levy fell short of 60% in 2022.

spending.basis: A yes vote funds 14 new firefighter/EMT positions and round-the-clock staffing at two more stations, which the district says will improve the level of EMS service, an expansion beyond current service.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7360 (S1); Fire District 3's EMS levy page and FAQ (S2, S3); Spokesman-Review coverage (S4); the 2022 EMS levy record and result (S5, S6); the 2023 levy lid lift record and result (S7, S8); RCW 84.52.069 (S9); PDC query (S10).

measures.what_it_does: Lifts Fire District 9's regular fire levy from about $0.65 to the legal maximum of $1.50 per $1,000 for 2027, then lets levy revenue grow up to 6% a year for five years (still capped at $1.50); the 2032 amount becomes the base for later years. The chief says about half the money would replace aging fire vehicles; the rest goes to equipment, personnel and operations.
measures.cost_line: The district estimates $423 more per year ($35.25 a month) on a $500,000 property in 2027, and levy revenue can rise up to 6% a year after that. The board has also promised to cut its separate M&O levy by $0.20 per $1,000 from 2028, which it says would make the net increase $323 a year; that promise is not part of the ballot measure.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor reached the pamphlet by the deadline (For committee contact Caroline Kusher). The district says calls have nearly doubled since 2013 and it has not asked for a regular levy increase in over 45 years. Chief Matthew Vinci calls new engines, brush trucks, tenders and a ladder truck 'must-haves.'
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote more than doubles the district's regular levy rate (about $0.65 to $1.50 per $1,000) and allows 6% annual revenue growth for five years. The promised $0.20 M&O cut is a board commitment, not part of the measure.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7361 (S1); Resolution 26-8 in the June 23, 2026 board packet (S2); June 23 and July 14, 2026 minutes (S3, S4); district flyer and newsletter (S5, S6); Spokesman-Review coverage (S7); 2024 M&O levy records and results (S8-S11); RCW 84.55.050 (S12); PDC query (S13).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes Fire District 9 to issue $70 million in 20-year bonds, repaid by a new property tax. The money would replace Station 99, renovate four other stations, build a training and classroom building, and expand the maintenance and logistics building.
measures.cost_line: $70,000,000 in bonds repaid over up to 20 years, at an estimated $0.39 per $1,000 of assessed value: about $196 a year ($16.34 a month) on a $500,000 property. This is on top of Proposition 1.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The district says its stations are outdated, have seen no significant improvements in more than 30 years, and do not meet the growing demand for fire, EMS, wildfire and rescue response.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a new excess property tax of about $0.39 per $1,000 for up to 20 years to repay $70 million in bonds. It does not replace an existing bond levy.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7362 (S1); Resolution 26-9 in the June 23, 2026 board packet (S2); June 23 and July 14, 2026 minutes (S3, S4); district newsletter (S5); Spokesman-Review coverage (S6); 2024 M&O levy record (S7); PDC query (S8).

measures.what_it_does: Renews Fire District 11's six-year emergency medical services levy for the area around Rockford. It restores the rate to the $0.35 per $1,000 voters approved in 2021, up from about $0.27 now.
measures.cost_line: $0.35 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 ($105 on a $300,000 home, about $25 more than the current rate). After 2027, revenue can grow only 1% a year.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The district says renewal is needed to maintain EMS supplies and equipment as costs rise. Chief Gary Hill says the rate was kept low on purpose as other taxes rise; $0.35 is below the 50-cent legal maximum.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews an expiring EMS levy and restores it to the $0.35 rate voters approved in 2021, a modest rise from about $0.27. It is a replacement, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7363 (S1); Spokesman-Review interview with Chief Gary Hill (S2); the 2021 EMS levy record and result (S3, S4); RCW 84.52.069 (S5).

measures.what_it_does: Renews Fire District 12's six-year emergency medical services levy for Latah, Waverly and the surrounding area, at its existing rate.
measures.cost_line: $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed value a year, collected 2027 through 2032 ($150 a year on a $300,000 home). This is the same rate voters approved in 2020.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The commissioners say the levy is necessary to provide emergency medical services to district residents.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; no volunteers came forward to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews the district's six-year EMS levy at the same $0.50 rate approved in 2020. It is a replacement, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7364 (S1); the 2020 EMS levy record and result (S2, S3); RCW 84.52.069 (S4); Spokesman-Review mention of Fire District 12 (S5). No district website or news coverage specific to the measure was found.

measures.what_it_does: Changes the County Council's meeting rule from at least once in each of 50 weeks a year to at least 45 meetings a year. Every meeting where law or rule requires public comment must offer remote attendance and remote public comment.
measures.cost_line: No fiscal statement was published, and no source estimates a cost.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Committee for Flexible Council Meetings: Troy Serad, Dick Muri, Dave Morell) says the amendment replaces 'a rigid scheduling rule with a more practical standard' and that writing remote comment into the Charter helps residents who cannot attend in person take part. It notes the Charter Review Commission sent it to the ballot with zero votes in opposition.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was submitted.
measures.sources_note: VoteWA voter-guide record 7313: ballot title, explanatory statement and statement for, with no statement against (S1). Gig Harbor Now on the commission's seven proposals (S2) and on how the commission works (S3). Tacoma Weekly ballot roundup (S4) and its sheriff-oversight story, which identifies council members (S5). PDC committee query (S6). The Pierce County local pamphlet could not be read (piercecountywa.gov returned HTTP 403).

measures.what_it_does: Makes the Sheriff an appointed office: the County Executive appoints and a council majority confirms. The current elected term, held by Sheriff Keith Swank since January 2025, would end on January 1, 2027, two years early.
measures.cost_line: No fiscal statement was published. Neither side makes a cost argument.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Pierce County for a Professional Sheriff: Nathe Lawver, Jake Hunter, Lyle Quasim) argues that a hiring process screens for credentials and a proven public-safety record rather than campaigning. It says an appointed sheriff can be put on leave or removed for serious misconduct, while an elected one stays until the next election.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Pierce County Citizens for Accountable Public Safety: Brian Sonntag, Bruce Dammeier, Paul Pastor) says the measure takes away voters' right to elect the sheriff and cuts short the term voters gave the current sheriff. It argues an appointed sheriff answers first to the Executive, and that voters can already remove a sheriff through elections, recall or prosecution.
measures.sources_note: VoteWA voter-guide record 7314: ballot title, explanatory statement, statements for and against, and rebuttals (S1). Gig Harbor Now (S2, S3), Seattle Times (S4), Center Square (S5, S8) and Tacoma Weekly (S6, S11, S13) on the commission's 12-9 vote, the sheriff's history and the controversy. MyNorthwest on the failed lawsuit (S7). Bolts (S9). KNKX on council candidates' positions (S10). PDC committees (S12). Axes considered and not mapped: safety and reform (the rubric does not apply them to measures) and local-control (authority stays inside county government).

measures.what_it_does: Creates a Public Safety Ombuds department to oversee the Sheriff's Office independently. The ombuds would investigate complaints, publish findings, refer cases to other authorities, and have subpoena power under the commission draft. The County Council appoints the ombuds from finalists chosen by a nominating panel. The amendment also requires a Community Advisory Committee.
measures.cost_line: No fiscal statement was published. The Charter requires funding and staffing but leaves the budget to a later ordinance. An opponent cited a roughly $1 million budget for a similar office in Spokane. Supporters cite claimed litigation savings.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Pierce County for Community Safety Oversight: Kate Ginn, Kristy Gledhill, Lyle Quasim) says complaints about the Sheriff's Office now go through slow, hard-to-navigate systems. It argues an ombuds with power to investigate, obtain records and subpoena witnesses would add accountability and transparency and catch problems before they become costly.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Pierce County Citizens for Accountable Public Safety: Brian Sonntag, Bruce Dammeier, Paul Pastor) says internal affairs, independent deadly-force teams, the state Office of Independent Investigations and the Criminal Justice Training Commission already provide oversight. It argues any new oversight should come by ordinance, not a permanent Charter department, and that resources should go to crime reduction and deputies.
measures.sources_note: VoteWA voter-guide record 7315: ballot title, explanatory statement, statements for and against, and rebuttals (S1). NWPB (S2, S3) and Tacoma Weekly (S4) on the draft's selection panel, subpoena power and the positions of the sheriff and the guild. Gig Harbor Now (S5). Center Square for Rogge's cost claims (S6). KNKX (S7). Tacoma Weekly roundup (S8). PDC (S9). Bolts (S10). News Tribune headline only (S11). Spending was considered and not mapped: the new department is itself oversight machinery, which the rubric's spending axis puts on the restraint pole, so the direction is ambiguous.

measures.what_it_does: Gives county initiative sponsors 180 days instead of 120 to collect signatures. The signature requirement stays at 10% of the votes in the last County Executive election, about 41,000 according to supporters.
measures.cost_line: No fiscal statement was published. Supporters say there is no cost to the county because campaigns pay for signature gathering.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Sharon Hanek, Mike Lonnergan, Grant Pelesky) says no county initiative has ever reached the Pierce County ballot under the 120-day limit. It argues two more months to collect over 40,000 signatures is fair, allows more mail outreach, and reduces reliance on paid signature gatherers.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Committee to Protect Our Initiative Process: Martha Lantz, Justin Leighton, Troy Serad) argues more time mainly helps well-funded interests pay for signature drives. It says the current system works, that several referendums have qualified within 120 days, and that voters have rejected such changes before.
measures.sources_note: VoteWA voter-guide record 7316: ballot title, explanatory statement, statements for and against, and rebuttals (S1). Gig Harbor Now (S2, S3). Tacoma Weekly roundup (S4). PDC (S5). Seattle Times identifies Hanek as a commissioner (S6). Reform (direct democracy) is the natural axis but does not apply to measures in the rubric, and both sides claim the anti-special-interest position.

measures.what_it_does: Requires the county's Chief Financial Officer to prepare a four-year budget outlook for each biennial budget. The outlook covers revenues, expenditures, reserves and fund balances for the Current Expense Fund and must show that projected spending will not exceed projected available funds. The Council must consider it when adopting the budget.
measures.cost_line: No fiscal statement was published. Opponents call it an unfunded mandate with no staff assigned. Supporters say no new staff or funding is needed because the finance office already prepares much of the outlook.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Wolf Opitz, Doug Richardson) says a four-year outlook would make county leaders show whether today's commitments are affordable later. It argues this reduces the risk of sudden cuts or rushed tax and fee increases and supports the county's credit rating.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Pierce County for Local Budget Control: Cameron Severns) says the amendment was meant to pair with companion proposal O-1, which was not sent to voters, so it assigns the duty to a position that does not exist. It calls the outlook duplicative of the existing biennial budget, six-year forecast and annual audit.

spending.basis: YES writes into the Charter a requirement that projected spending not exceed projected available funds over four years, framed by supporters as fiscal discipline (affordability, avoiding rushed tax and fee increases, protecting the credit rating). That is the rubric's audit-and-restrain pole. Strength is 1, not 2, because it is a planning and certification duty with no enforcement mechanism described, and the opposition also argues on restraint grounds.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voter-guide record 7317: ballot title, explanatory statement, statements for and against, and rebuttals (S1). Gig Harbor Now, which adds that the Council must 'consider the outlook' (S2). Tacoma Weekly roundup (S3). PDC: no committee found for or against (S4). Whether the Charter now has a Chief Financial Officer position could not be checked.

measures.what_it_does: Rewrites the Charter's nondiscrimination clause, which now lists race, creed, color, sex, age and handicap. The new list: sex, race, color, national origin or ancestry, creed, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age, genetic testing results, family caregiver status, pregnancy, childbirth or lactation, and military or veteran status. It adds that the clause may not impair rights under the U.S. or state constitution.
measures.cost_line: No fiscal statement was published. Each side says the other's position invites litigation, and neither gives a figure.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Pierce County for Aligned Employment Practices: Devin Rydel-Kelly, Latasha Palmer, Ayanna Colman) says the section has not been updated since 1980. It argues that aligning it with current law protects workers such as veteran families and caregivers, gives clear direction to a county workforce of over 3,000, and prevents costly lawsuits.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Common Sense for Pierce County: Mason Fletcher, Hollie Rogge, Jeff Joseph) says the existing clause already prohibits discrimination. It argues new terms such as genetic testing results and lactation are vague and invite litigation, and that the Charter should stay neutral rather than 'impose values that represent the few.' Its rebuttal also says the amendment removes veterans' preference, a claim this research could not verify.

social.basis: YES adds sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (plus pregnancy, childbirth and lactation) to the Charter's nondiscrimination clause, which is the rubric's pole B ('broad anti-discrimination law'). Opponents frame it as imposing values, and the sheriff testified against the gender-identity language. Strength is 1, not 2, because the measure bundles categories outside this axis and supporters present it as aligning with existing law rather than creating new protections.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voter-guide record 7318: ballot title, explanatory statement, statements for and against, and rebuttals (S1). Gig Harbor Now for the current Charter text and the sheriff's testimony (S2). Tacoma Weekly roundup (S3). Center Square on the sheriff's pronoun statement (S4). PDC (S5). MyNorthwest on the con signers (S6). Bolts (S7). The full amendment text was not available, so the veterans'-preference claim is unverified.

measures.what_it_does: Creates a Juvenile Detention Advocate Office within Pierce County Juvenile Detention to take complaints from detained youth and their families, monitor conditions, and handle mandatory-reporter rules. It also contributes data on use of force, room confinement and other operations to the Superior Court's annual reports. Juvenile Detention would get an independent audit or accreditation review at least once every five years.
measures.cost_line: No fiscal statement was published. Opponents say the new office will raise costs and supporters say oversight failures are costly, but neither side gives a figure.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Committee for Safe Youth, Strong Oversight: Justin Leighton, Rick Talbert, Hunter George) says every child in county custody deserves protection from abuse. It cites News Tribune investigations showing oversight failures harmed youth and cost taxpayers, and argues that independent oversight, public reporting and regular outside reviews belong permanently in the Charter.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Brenda Milewski) calls the office an unnecessary layer of government that adds cost. It argues Juvenile Detention has already improved and serves few youth, that the greatest need is a modern facility, and that the office could open the door to executive influence over a court function. Its rebuttal says existing Juvenile Court reforms already provide accountability.
measures.sources_note: VoteWA voter-guide record 7319: ballot title, explanatory statement, statements for and against, and rebuttals (S1). Gig Harbor Now on how the office is appointed and supervised (S2) and on the commission (S9). Tacoma Weekly roundup (S3). PDC (S4). News Tribune and KING5 headlines on Remann Hall abuse claims (S5-S8), headline only because the articles could not be retrieved. Spending was considered and not mapped: oversight machinery versus new government, so the direction is ambiguous.

measures.what_it_does: Raises Milton's sales and use tax by 0.1% starting in 2027 to fund police and public safety under RCW 82.14.450. It has no expiration date, and 15% of the proceeds go to the county.
measures.cost_line: Increases the sales and use tax by one-tenth of one percent (0.001), or 10 cents on a $100 taxable purchase; the city estimates about $200,000 a year. The combined rate in the Pierce County part of Milton would go from 10.2% to 10.3% (King County part: 10.3% to 10.4%).
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Dave Strader, Jacki Strader) says the tax will let the Milton Police Department 'maintain its current budget and high-quality services' as staffing, jail, court and other costs rise. It says the tax will ease pressure on the General Fund and protect funding for streets and parks.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was submitted. The mayor told the council in August that no one had volunteered for the 'Against' committee.

taxes.basis: A yes vote creates a new, open-ended 0.1% public safety sales tax. The city's staff report says neither King nor Pierce County levies this tax now. This matches the King scoring of the same measure.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA ballot title, explanatory statement and statement in favor (S1); Milton council packets with the staff report, budget figures, Resolution 26-2005 and the 6-0 vote (S2, S3); DOR Q4 2026 rates (S4); RCW 82.14.450 (S5); PDC query showing no committees (S6). Built from the King dossier of the same measure, with sources re-fetched. No news coverage was found, and the Pierce County pamphlet could not be read (HTTP 403).

measures.what_it_does: Lifts South Prairie's property tax levy limit so the town can raise its regular levy by about $1.33 per $1,000, to as much as $2.90 in 2027, for police, fire, EMS, parks, roads and other town services. It lets the levy grow up to 6% a year through 2032, and the 2032 amount becomes the base for later levies.
measures.cost_line: About $1.33 more per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027, or about $50 a month on a $450,000 home (town estimate), up to a maximum rate of $2.90 per $1,000. That implies a current town rate of about $1.57.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (David Brubaker, Dean Moerer) says the levy keeps core public safety and town services running as costs rise. It calls it a 'limited six-year measure' that is 'not about expanding government.'
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was submitted.

taxes.basis: A yes vote raises the town's regular levy by about $1.33 per $1,000 from an implied $1.57, roughly an 85% increase. The ballot title keeps the 2032 levy amount as the base for later levies, so this is a large lid lift that carries forward.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA ballot title, explanatory statement and statement in favor (S1); 2018 Courier-Herald article on the town's permanent EMS levy (S2); PDC query showing no committees (S3). No 2026 news coverage was found, the town website has no levy material, and the Pierce County pamphlet could not be read (HTTP 403).

measures.what_it_does: Raises Pierce Transit's dedicated sales tax from 0.6% to 0.9% starting April 1, 2027, its first increase since 2002. The money pays for a planned 47% service expansion: four new routes, more frequent buses, later hours, special event service, expanded paratransit, and free fares for seniors.
measures.cost_line: An additional 0.3% sales and use tax, 3 cents on a $10 taxable purchase, with no end date; it does not apply to groceries, rent, most healthcare, gas or utilities. In Tacoma the combined rate would go from 10.5% to 10.8%.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Alice Phillips, Faaluaina Pritchard, Krystal Monteros) says transit is how many people reach jobs and appointments. It says the measure is the first local transit investment since 2002, increases service by 47%, makes seniors ride free and keeps youth fares free.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (John Miles) says 'the sales tax is too high': Tacoma would reach 10.8%, higher sales taxes hit the poor hardest, and legislators should find another funding source. It agrees that more service is needed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote raises Pierce Transit's sales tax rate by half, from 0.6% to 0.9%, with no expiration. The opposition argues against the sales tax increase itself.

spending.basis: The new revenue pays for a 47% service expansion with new routes, longer hours and new fare-free service for seniors, not only for preserving current service.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA ballot title, explanatory statement, statements and rebuttals (S1); Pierce Transit's ballot measure site and October 2026 presentation (S2, S3); Urbanist coverage of the board vote and the expansion plan (S4, S5); DOR Q4 2026 rates (S6); PDC records for Keep Pierce Moving, the only registered committee (S7-S9). No revenue estimate was found, and the Pierce County pamphlet could not be read (HTTP 403).

measures.what_it_does: A citizen initiative that adds enforcement to Tacoma's tenant protection laws. It recognizes tenant unions and requires most landlords to bargain with them, lets tenants file city complaints or sue, and sets penalties of $500 to five times monthly rent that go to the affected tenants. It also requires all landlords to get rental licenses and pay per-unit fees, creates a public landlord database, and allows license revocation for dangerous violations.
measures.cost_line: No tax; the program is funded by a per-unit rental license fee capped at the city's enforcement costs, with higher fees for large landlords and repeat offenders. Opponents cite an $8-10 million annual city cost and a $191 per-unit fee; supporters say similar programs charge $10-35 per unit. No published city estimate was found.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Tyron Moore, Kiss'Shonna Curtis, Bill Hanawalt) says the measure holds 'outside corporate slumlords' accountable for illegal rent hikes and mold, protects renters from retaliation when they organize, and makes repeat violators and corporate landlords pay for enforcement instead of taxpayers.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Michael Mirra, Ben Lackey, Mark Melsness) says the measure creates an $8-10 million licensing bureaucracy during a $40 million budget shortfall, that licensing fees will raise rents and make housing harder to build, and that Tacoma already has strong renter protections.

spending.basis: It requires the city to build a new enforcement program (complaint adjudication, inspections, licensing, a landlord database), funded by fees. Opponents object to its cost amid a budget shortfall.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA ballot title, explanatory statement, statements and rebuttals (S1); Tacoma For All campaign pages, FAQ, endorsements and the initiative text it posts (S2-S5); KNKX and Cascade PBS coverage (S6, S7); City of Tacoma Ordinance 29086 release and the initiative process page (S8, S9); PDC records for Tacoma for All PAC, No on Initiative 1 and the Rental Housing Association PAC (S10-S16). The News Tribune and the Pierce County pamphlet could not be read, and no city fiscal estimate was found.

measures.what_it_does: Renews Riverside Fire & Rescue's (Fire District 14) emergency medical services property tax levy for six more years, 2027 through 2032, at up to $0.50 per $1,000. The 2020 levy expires at the end of 2026.
measures.cost_line: Up to $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed value, the same maximum as the expiring levy: no more than $50 a year ($4.17 a month) per $100,000 of assessed value.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Riverside Firefighters For EMS: Holly Leiter, Dustin Garrett, Ethan Longknife) says the levy is 'not a new tax' but a continuation. It says call volume is rising and the levy keeps staffing, equipment and emergency care at current levels.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was submitted.

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews an expiring EMS property tax at the same $0.50 maximum for six years. It is a renewal, not a new tax or a rate increase.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA ballot title, explanatory statement and statement in favor (S1); the district's site with the Resolution 2026-416 notice and its service area (S2, S3); PDC query showing no committees (S4). The pro statement calls this an 'M&O levy' although the ballot describes an EMS levy. No news coverage was found, and the Pierce County pamphlet could not be read (HTTP 403).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes Auburn School District to issue up to $491 million in 20-year bonds to build a new Middle School #5 and replace Cascade Middle School and Alpac Elementary with larger schools. The same three schools were in bonds that failed to reach the required 60% in 2024 (a larger $532.1 million package, 55%) and 2025 ($490 million, 54%).
measures.cost_line: Up to $491,000,000 in bonds repaid by excess property taxes. The district estimates an average of $1.10 per $1,000 of assessed value, about $55 a month on a $600,000 home. Pierce County property in the district is assessed by the Pierce County Assessor.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Cari Manry, Terri Herren) says the bond would end middle-school overcrowding (more than 1,100 students in 45 portables), replace aging buildings at about $1.10 per $1,000, and secure state matching funds, noting that a majority voted yes last time.
measures.con_summary: The statement in opposition (Eric Petersen) says $163 million per school is excessive next to Tacoma's costs. It says repaying principal plus $350+ million in interest pushes the real rate to $1.93 per $1,000, and it asks voters to make the district resubmit a smaller request.

taxes.basis: A yes vote authorizes a new $491 million bond, not a renewal. The district projects its combined bond rate rising from $1.50 (2026) to $2.53 (2027-2031) per $1,000, and the con case is about tax burden. This matches the King scoring of the same measure.

spending.basis: Besides replacing two schools, the bond builds a fifth middle school to add capacity. The opposition argues for a smaller, cheaper request.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA ballot title, explanatory statement, statements and rebuttals (S1; the two rebuttals are stored in swapped fields); district election page, Q&A (which refers exemptions to the King and Pierce assessors) and Election Information Book with the King/Pierce vote splits and rate tables (S2-S4); Auburn Reporter coverage of 2024-2026 (S5-S7); PDC records for Auburn Citizen's for Schools (S8, S9). Built from the King dossier of the same measure, with sources re-fetched.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes Yelm Community Schools to collect a two-year educational programs and operations levy: $11.2 million in 2027 and $12.3 million in 2028. The district has had no local levy since 2024; this one would keep current programs, staff and athletics; the district says it would also restore some cut programs, which opponents dispute. The district says that if it fails, the state would take financial oversight of the district.
measures.cost_line: An estimated $1.50 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027 and 2028 ($11,194,449 and $12,278,072), on tax bills that now carry no Yelm EP&O levy; about $600 a year on a $400,000 home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Yelm Kids First: Judson Willis, Debbie Edwards, Kathryn Cullum) says repeated levy failures have already forced cuts to staff, programs and athletics. It says the state does not fully fund schools and the levy is needed to restore stability and keep student programs.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Martin Miller, Frank Vance) says voters have said no four times and the district restores none of the cut programs. It says the district used one-time money for recurring costs, and argues for controlling expenses and taking the funding fight to Olympia instead of 'neighbors tax neighbors.'

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a $1.50 per $1,000 levy (about $11-12 million a year) where none has been collected since 2024; OSPI lists Yelm with $0 in local levy funding for 2026. This is a new levy, not a replacement, though it lasts only two years. The con case is explicitly about not raising taxes.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA ballot title, explanatory statement, statements and rebuttals (S1); the district's levy page, levy FAQ, fiscal-oversight FAQ and school-funding page (S2-S5); OSPI 2026 levy status data (S6); PDC records for Yelm Kids First and the 2026 committee query (S7-S9). Local news (Nisqually Valley News) and the Pierce County pamphlet could not be read (HTTP 403). No parental-rights content.

measures.what_it_does: Limits County Council members to three consecutive four-year terms (12 years), counting prior consecutive service; a former member may run again after one full term out of office.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate in the ballot title; amends the Clark County Home Rule Charter.
measures.pro_summary: Brandon Erickson, Dorothy Gasque and Liz Shaw: open seats widen the field and bring fresh perspectives; twelve years is ample time to serve, and former members may run again after a term away.
measures.con_summary: Morgan Holmgren, Liz Cline and Chuck Green: voters already remove councilors who overstay; limits cost institutional knowledge, empower unelected staff and interest groups, and restrict voter choice.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record (local pamphlet statements, S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); Charter Review Commission page (S4).

measures.what_it_does: Writes an earlier county budget calendar into the charter: earlier department estimates, preliminary budget information from the County Manager, and public presentations (September and October) before a November adoption hearing.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate in the ballot title; amends the Clark County Home Rule Charter.
measures.pro_summary: Peter Silliman, Liz Cline and Ann Donnelly: moves the first public budget presentation to early September and adoption to November, giving residents time to review a budget of almost $900 million.
measures.con_summary: John Latta, Julie Koepp and Janet Landesberg: the charter already lets the county set earlier deadlines; process details do not belong in the charter and would make the budget process harder to improve.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record (local pamphlet statements, S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); Charter Review Commission page (S4).

measures.what_it_does: Lets the County Council nominate members to all county boards and commissions alongside the County Manager, except the Ethics Review Commission; today it nominates to three.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate in the ballot title; amends the Clark County Home Rule Charter.
measures.pro_summary: Patrick Adigweme and Eric LaBrant: the Council can now nominate only to three bodies; letting councilors nominate volunteers to the rest could help keep seats filled.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed: after recruitment attempts, no one in the jurisdiction volunteered to write one.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record (local pamphlet statements, S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); Charter Review Commission page (S4).

measures.what_it_does: County nonpartisan races (Council, Assessor, Auditor, Clerk, Sheriff, Treasurer, Prosecuting Attorney) with one or two candidates would skip the August primary and go straight to the general; county elections stay in even-numbered years.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate in the ballot title; amends the Clark County Home Rule Charter.
measures.pro_summary: Cathie Garber, Jennifer Wendel and Dorothy Gasque: a primary with one or two candidates narrows nothing; skipping it, as other nonpartisan races already do, saves printing and mailing costs.
measures.con_summary: Ann Donnelly, Peter Silliman and Liz Cline: the primary and its pamphlet inform voters for months; skipping it favors incumbents and embeds even-year elections in the charter.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record (local pamphlet statements, S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); Charter Review Commission page (S4).

measures.what_it_does: Requires the County Manager to present and broadly publish an annual statement of the county's fiscal and governmental affairs (now optional), and to present the budget in a public meeting.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate in the ballot title; amends the Clark County Home Rule Charter.
measures.pro_summary: Patrick Adigweme, Eric LaBrant and Ann Donnelly: makes the annual report mandatory and broadly published, so the public gets it regardless of who holds office.
measures.con_summary: Margaret Tweet: the 'publish broadly' mandate has no election-season limit and could fund mailers that favor incumbents or county ballot measures; post reports online instead.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record (local pamphlet statements, S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); Charter Review Commission page (S4).

measures.what_it_does: Requires the county to publish a Housing Impact Analysis before adopting any discretionary ordinance likely to materially affect housing capacity, density, permitting, subdivisions, residential parking or construction costs.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate in the ballot title; amends the Clark County Home Rule Charter.
measures.pro_summary: John Jay, David Stuebe and Justin Wood: councilors and the public should see the housing-cost effects of discretionary land-use rules before adoption; it dictates no outcome.
measures.con_summary: Chuck Green, Irene Finley and Morgan Holmgren: policy micromanagement in the charter; reports cost taxpayers and will not fix affordability driven by interest rates and state and federal rules.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record (local pamphlet statements, S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); Charter Review Commission page (S4).

measures.what_it_does: From 2027, a new or increased council-imposed (councilmanic) tax would need a two-thirds Council vote, which on a five-member council means four votes. Fees, special assessments and renewals at the same rate are excluded.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate in the ballot title; amends the Clark County Home Rule Charter.
measures.pro_summary: John Jay, Paul Harris and Brian Lewallen: new council-imposed taxes should need broad agreement; it changes no current tax or service.
measures.con_summary: Janet Landesberg, Dorothy Gasque and Julie Koepp: on a five-member council two-thirds means four votes, letting two councilors block funding for law and justice, roads and parks.

taxes.basis: YES requires four of five councilors to approve any new or increased council-imposed tax, a structural limit on tax increases; Snohomish's four-of-five tax supermajority amendment maps the same way.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record (local pamphlet statements, S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); Charter Review Commission page (S4).

measures.what_it_does: Lowers the signatures needed for county initiatives and referenda from 10% to 8%, lets a short initiative become a mini-initiative, simplifies the count for unincorporated-area measures, and allows statistical sampling to verify signatures.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate in the ballot title; amends the Clark County Home Rule Charter.
measures.pro_summary: Cathie Garber, Liz Cline and Dorothy Gasque: no citizen petition has qualified since 2014; a lower threshold and signature sampling keep safeguards while making the process achievable.
measures.con_summary: Janet Landesberg and Chuck Green: voters rejected the same thresholds in 2022 by 59%; every signature should be verified, and lower thresholds elsewhere produced no initiatives.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record (local pamphlet statements, S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); Charter Review Commission page (S4). 2022 Charter Amendment No. 14 record and results (S5, S6).

measures.what_it_does: Lets the County Council order independent performance and program audits of county operations and requires it to set up an independent auditing process by ordinance; state audits continue.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate in the ballot title; amends the Clark County Home Rule Charter.
measures.pro_summary: Peter Silliman, Liz Cline and Ann Donnelly: the body that approves department budgets should be able to commission performance audits, as other charter counties allow.
measures.con_summary: John Latta, Dijana Katan and Janet Landesberg: councilors and residents can already request audits and the State Auditor reviews for free; the measure's fiscal analysis says it could cost at least $100,000 more a year.

spending.basis: YES gives the Council power to commission independent performance and program audits, the oversight-and-audit pole; it authorizes audits rather than restraining any budget.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record (local pamphlet statements, S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); Charter Review Commission page (S4).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes up to $366,204,000 in 31-year general obligation bonds to remodel and expand the Clark County Jail, add courtrooms and build or remodel the Sheriff's Office headquarters, repaid by a countywide excess property tax.
measures.cost_line: Up to $366,204,000 in bonds over up to 31 years, repaid by a new countywide excess property tax; supporters estimate about $86 a year for a median home. No rate is stated in the ballot title.
measures.pro_summary: Ann Donnelly, Sue Marshall and John Horch: the jail, built more than 40 years ago, is overcrowded and unsafe; expansion would add treatment and reentry space and cut the cost of housing inmates elsewhere.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed: after recruitment attempts, no one in the jurisdiction volunteered to write one.

taxes.basis: YES adds a new 31-year countywide excess property-tax levy to repay up to $366 million in bonds.

spending.basis: YES funds a large capital expansion: more jail capacity, added courtrooms and a new or remodeled Sheriff's headquarters.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record 7342 (S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3).

measures.what_it_does: Lifts the county's regular property-tax levy to $1.15 per $1,000 in 2027 (about $0.44 more) to pay for more corrections officers, sheriff's deputies and prosecutors; the 2027 amount becomes the base for later years.
measures.cost_line: County levy up to $1.15 per $1,000 in 2027, about $0.44 (62%) more than 2026: about $264 more on a $600,000 property, per the statement against; supporters put the cost at about $212 a year per median household.
measures.pro_summary: Ann Donnelly, Sue Marshall and John Horch: the Sheriff's Office has one of the lowest deputy-to-population ratios in the state; the levy funds deputies, corrections officers and prosecutors.
measures.con_summary: Margaret Tweet: a 62% jump in the county levy rate, raised to staff a jail expansion voters have not yet approved, on top of a 0.1% criminal justice sales tax the Council adopted in April 2026.

taxes.basis: YES raises the county regular levy from about $0.71 to $1.15 per $1,000 (about 62%) and makes the 2027 amount the base for future limits.

spending.basis: YES pays for additional deputies, corrections officers and prosecutors, expanding staffing beyond current service.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record 7344 (S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3).

measures.what_it_does: Restores Battle Ground Public Schools' educational programs and operations levy, which expired in 2025, for 2027-2029: safety, smaller classes, special education, reading and math support, curriculum and activities.
measures.pro_summary: Terry Dotson and Sabrena Worthy: replaces the levy that expired in 2025, lowering the amount from the failed proposals as the community asked; failure risks state financial oversight.
measures.con_summary: Richard Rylander: the fourth attempt after three failures; about $1,144 a year on a $650,000 home, with no line-item commitment on how the general-fund money is spent.

taxes.basis: YES restores a lapsed operations levy at an estimated $1.76 per $1,000, below the $1.95 the district sought in April 2025.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure record 7345 (S1); sample ballot (S2); county election page (S3); April 2025 Prop 9 record (S4) and results (S5); February 2025 results (S6).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes a three-year South Kitsap School District capital levy (2027-2029) for elementary security cameras, intercoms, entrance access controls and bus radios, student Chromebooks and cybersecurity, a high school theater renovation and gym bleachers, and synthetic turf fields at South Kitsap High and Marcus Whitman Middle School. Passes with a simple majority.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $1.50 per $1,000 of assessed value: $23.5 million (2027), $24.2 million (2028) and $24.9 million (2029), $72.6 million in total. That is about $750 a year on a $500,000 home (the district rounds to $756). It is not described as replacing an expiring levy and would be collected alongside the district's EP&O levy.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Katherine Ander and Carl Olson, South Kitsap School Supporters) says the state does not pay for most school repairs or technology, and that even the newest schools are over 30 years old. It says the money must stay in South Kitsap for voter-approved projects, and acting now avoids costlier failures later.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed. The Auditor's Office recruited by text, email, press release and social media, and no one came forward.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a new three-year property tax of about $1.50 per $1,000 ($72.6 million). No source describes it as replacing an expiring levy, and the district has no bond debt. Whether any of the 2018 capital levy is still being collected was not found; if it were, that would argue for +1.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7380 (S1); the district's levy page and flyer (S2-S3); South Kitsap School Supporters (S4); Kitsap Daily News / Port Orchard Independent coverage of the 2026 levy (S5-S6), the 2018 capital levy (S7), the district's 2024 plans after the failed bond (S8), and the 2026 campaign (S9). A Kitsap Sun story was paywalled (HTTP 402) and not used.

measures.what_it_does: Asks whether Kitsap Public Utility District (KPUD), now a water, wastewater and fiber utility, may build or buy electric generation, transmission or distribution facilities. Puget Sound Energy serves the county today. A yes vote gives KPUD that authority permanently with no second public vote required, though it does not have to use it. The board has committed to a feasibility study first, and if PSE will not sell, KPUD could seek to acquire the system through condemnation. A no vote ends the current effort.
measures.cost_line: No tax, rate or bond in the ballot title. KPUD says property taxes and rates would not change because of the vote. A yes vote does trigger the board's promised feasibility study, estimated at $300,000-$500,000. The cost of any later acquisition is unknown; Jefferson PUD paid $103 million for PSE's much smaller Jefferson County system in 2010.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (David Behar, William Woznicki and Sue Ellen White) says a yes vote allows a transparent study of public power, and the effort stops if the numbers don't work. It argues PUD rates run below PSE's, that money paid to PSE shareholders could stay local, and that decisions would be closer to ratepayers.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Varon Mullis, Robert P. McGee and Shannon Turner, Citizens for Accountable Utilities in Kitsap) says the measure grants broad, permanent authority to buy or build a utility before any cost evidence, with no second vote. It notes that similar measures failed in Skagit, Island and Thurston counties, and that KPUD can study costs without this vote.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7376 (S1); KPUD's Exploring Electric Service page, Prop 1 fact publication, Resolution 26-07-28A, the June 22, 2026 general manager memo, an Oct. 7 presentation and a July listening-session post (S2-S7); Kitsap Daily News coverage including PSE's response (S8); RCW 54.08.070 and 54.16.040 (S9-S10). No lean: the measure raises no tax and authorizes no spending, and the local-control reading (state-regulated private utility versus locally governed public one) does not fit the rubric's poles. Kitsap Sun stories were paywalled (HTTP 402) and not used.

measures.what_it_does: Lifts Timberland Regional Library's regular property tax levy from about $0.22 to $0.35 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 and 2028; the 2028 amount becomes the base for later limits. TRL says about 96% of its budget comes from this levy, and that the money would restore open hours, staffing, collections and programs after 2026 budget cuts. The measure is decided by the combined vote of all five TRL counties.
measures.cost_line: From $0.228924 to $0.35 per $1,000 of assessed value, about $14 million more in 2027. Estimates for a Thurston home range from about $40 a year on a $334,000 home (explanatory statement) to $59 a year on the $457,400 median (TRL) and $69 a year on a $530,959 home (statement for).
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (TimberStrong Libraries Committee) says the levy has not risen in 25 years and has been eroded by rising costs, and that approval would restore hours and staffing and expand collections and programs: 'a long overdue cost-of-living raise.'
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Sean Swope, Citizens for Accountable TR Libraries) says property owners already face rising bills, and that the library should first show it has cut costs, sought grants and managed existing resources better. It says a no vote 'is not a vote against libraries or literacy.'

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a levy lid lift, which the taxes pole_b names explicitly: it raises TRL's regular levy rate by more than half, from about $0.22 (exactly $0.228924) to $0.35 per $1,000, adding about $14 million in 2027.

spending.basis: A yes vote funds more open hours, staffing, collections and programs after recent cuts, against an opposing case that the library should first cut costs and prove prudent management.

measures.sources_note: Local voters' pamphlet pages 24-25 (S1) and sample ballot (S2); Auditor's past-results list (S3); TRL levy page, Q&A and board news release (S4-S6); JOLT, Nisqually Valley News, Daily World and Chronicle coverage (S7-S11); PDC queries (S12-S13). The outcome of Olympia's Oct. 6 support resolution was not confirmed.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes a two-year educational programs and operations (EP&O) levy for Yelm Community Schools, which has had no local levy for 2025 and 2026 after four failed attempts. It would keep the programs in place in 2025-26, such as current class sizes, AP and electives, athletics, activities, nurses, security and school resource officers,. The district says a limited amount would also let the board bring back some cut programs, and that if the levy fails the state would move it into financial oversight.
measures.cost_line: Up to $11,194,449 in 2027 and $12,278,072 in 2028, at an estimated $1.50 per $1,000 of assessed value. That is the lowest rate that qualifies for full state levy equalization; the legal maximum is $2.50. No Yelm EP&O levy is being collected now, so this adds a tax to current bills.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Yelm Kids First) says that after repeated levy failures the district has already cut staff, programs and athletics, and that the levy pays for teachers, counselors, nurses, safety staff and activities the state does not fully fund.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Martin Miller and Frank Vance) says voters have said no four times and the levy restores none of the cuts. It says the district used one-time capital money for recurring costs, and that residents should press Olympia to meet its 'paramount duty' instead of taxing neighbors.

taxes.basis: No Yelm EP&O levy is being collected in 2025 or 2026. A yes vote brings back an excess levy of an estimated $1.50 per $1,000, about $11.2 million in 2027 and $12.3 million in 2028, so relative to current bills it is a new tax rather than a like-for-like renewal.

measures.sources_note: Local voters' pamphlet pages 26-27 (S1) and sample ballot (S2); Auditor's past-results list and 2025 SOS results (S3, S11); district levy FAQ (S4); Nisqually Valley News coverage 2025-2026 (S5-S10); PDC query (S12). parental-rights is not mapped: the sources describe staffing, programs and operations, not notification, records or opt-outs.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes Lacey Fire District 3 to issue up to $98.3 million in general obligation bonds, repaid by property taxes over up to 20 years. The money would build a new station north of I-5 (Britton Pkwy), replace Station 32 on the Yelm Highway corridor, and build a regional live fire training facility and a logistics warehouse, plus property, other capital improvements and apparatus. The district cites more than 18,000 calls a year and only one of five stations north of I-5.
measures.cost_line: About $0.23 per $1,000 of assessed value, or about $9.60 a month on a $500,000 home, per the explanatory statement; the district's fact sheet gives $0.22 to $0.25 ($8 to $11 a month). Bond money cannot pay salaries or operations.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Steve Brooks and Tom Carroll) says calls are up 43% in ten years, a disaster could cut off the area north of I-5, and building now avoids higher construction costs later.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; the pamphlet says no one in the jurisdiction contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a new excess property tax of about $0.23 per $1,000 (about $9.60 a month on a $500,000 home) for up to 20 years to repay $98.3 million in capital bonds. It is a moderate new tax for capital projects, not an operating levy.

spending.basis: A yes vote funds new public capital beyond current service: a new station north of I-5 to close a response coverage gap, plus a new regional live fire training facility and a logistics warehouse, sized for 20 years of growth.

measures.sources_note: Local voters' pamphlet page 28 (S1; the page also carries a stray 'Fire Protection District 12' heading and ballot title left over from the November 2025 pamphlet, see S11) and sample ballot (S2); Auditor's past-results list (S3); district bond page and fact sheet (S4-S5); JOLT coverage (S6-S9); PDC query (S10). The outcome of Lacey's Oct. 6 support resolution was not confirmed, and the remaining term of the 2017 bond was not found.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes the West Thurston Regional Fire Authority (Rochester and Littlerock) to collect a one-year excess maintenance and operations levy in 2027. The ballot title covers maintenance and operations to keep current fire and EMS service. The authority cites failing apparatus, a facility water system replacement and an aging fleet, and the statement for says all the money will go to apparatus replacement and facility maintenance. Earlier M&O levies failed in 2022 and 2024, and the August 2026 levies were short of 60% on election night.
measures.cost_line: $1,547,228 in 2027, about $0.36 per $1,000 of assessed value: at most $15 a month ($180 a year) on a $500,000 home. Needs 60% approval.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Tyler Mason and Cathe Linn) says many frontline vehicles are at or past their service life, and that stations need HVAC, roof, electrical and plumbing work. It says replacing equipment before it fails costs less than waiting for emergencies.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; the pamphlet says no one in the jurisdiction contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a one-year excess levy of about $0.36 per $1,000 on top of the regular fire levy. Recent M&O levies failed, so it adds to current bills, but it is small and lasts one year.

measures.sources_note: Local voters' pamphlet page 29 (S1) and sample ballot (S2); Auditor's past-results list and SOS 2022/2024 results (S3-S5); WTRFA Strategic Plan 2026-2030 (S6); Chronicle coverage of the August 2026 levies (S7-S8); PDC query (S9). Certified August 2026 results were not retrieved.

measures.what_it_does: Amends the Bellingham city charter to drop the rule that the mayor must be paid at least as much as the highest-paid city employee, and has the city's independent salary commission set the mayor's salary instead. The commission already sets City Council pay.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate. The commission would set the salary; no figure is stated. The mayor now makes just under $237,000 a year plus about $49,000 in benefits.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Mayor Kim Lund and Edwin "Skip" Williams) says the current formula ratchets the mayor's pay up as staff wages rise, that Bellingham is the 'lone outlier' among similar Washington cities, and that a commission is the same transparent process used for the council and county officials.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no committee against formed. In a March guest column written before the measure was proposed, Andrew Reding argued that salary commissions' decisions are final and lack public accountability, though he also urged repealing the mayor-pay formula.
measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7295 (S1); Cascadia Daily News on the proposal and the unanimous council vote (S2); March 2026 CDN guest columns on salary commissions by Andrew Reding (S3) and RB Tewksbury (S4). A change in who sets one official's pay; no rubric measure axis applies.

measures.what_it_does: Amends the Bellingham city charter so the mayor can name a designee to sign city contracts, ends the requirement that the finance director attest the mayor's signature and affix the city seal, and allows electronic signatures.
measures.cost_line: No tax or rate. The city says a paperless process would save time and money but gives no figure.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Mayor Kim Lund and Edwin "Skip" Williams) says every contract now has to be printed, mailed and hand-signed by at least four officials before the seal is crimped on, which 'adds time and cost to every contract without adding value or accountability.'
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed, no committee against formed, and no published opposition was found.
measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7297 (S1); one paragraph of Cascadia Daily News coverage (S2). Administrative charter change; no rubric measure axis applies.

measures.what_it_does: A citizen initiative that bans landlords in Bellingham from agreeing on rents or paying for software that pools rental data from multiple landlords to recommend rents, lease terms or occupancy. It lets injured tenants sue, lets the City Attorney enforce, sets fines and possible misdemeanor penalties, and protects whistleblowers. Hotels and short-term rentals are exempt.
measures.cost_line: No tax or fee. Penalties include up to $5,000 per violation, triple damages in civil suits, and up to 90 days in jail for willful or repeat violations.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Community First Whatcom: Seth Mangold, Eukia Lemaster, Finn Kurtz) says shared pricing software lets landlords raise rents together, which would be illegal price-fixing if people did it, and cites an average $70 a month more for algorithmically priced units. It says Seattle, Portland and other cities have similar bans.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no opposing committee was found. In a CDN guest column, Kevin Donnelly of the Real Estate Technology and Transformation Center argued that rents are high because housing supply is short, that the software often recommends lower rents, and that Bellingham should loosen zoning rules instead. The initiative's own findings say the practice 'is currently not known to be a common practice in Bellingham.'
measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7298 (S1); Community First Whatcom's page with the full initiative text (S2); Cascadia Daily News coverage of the signature drive (S3, S4) and an opposing guest column (S5); PDC record for the sponsoring committee (S6). A tenant and rental-market regulation; the rubric's housing axis does not apply to measures and no measure axis fits.

measures.what_it_does: Raises the City of Lynden's regular property tax rate by about 50 cents, to $1.54304 per $1,000, for collection in 2027, then lets the levy grow 3% a year through 2035. The money would go to police and fire, street and park maintenance, the community/senior center, restoring cut staff, and reopening City Hall on Fridays.
measures.cost_line: Up from about $1.04 to $1.54304 per $1,000: about $300 a year more on a $600,000 home, raising about $2 million a year. After 2027 the levy may grow 3% a year through 2035.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Committee For Lynden Proposition #1: Kevin Pawlowski, Jonathan Abramson, Robert Libolt) says the city has already cut costs in every department, needs more police as it grows, and has a fire department handling over 2,700 calls a year; it calls the 50-cent increase 'a small additional amount.'
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no committee against formed. Council member Nick Laninga voted against placing it on the ballot. Council member Gary Bode voted yes but noted the burden of rising state and federal taxes.

taxes.basis: A yes vote raises the city's levy rate by about 48%, from about $1.04 to $1.54304 per $1,000, then allows 3% annual growth through 2035 with a permanent new base. It is a new increase, not a renewal.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide measure 7299 (S1); the City of Lynden's levy lid lift page and spending plan (S2); Cascadia Daily News (S3) and Lynden Tribune (S4, S5) coverage of the council vote; PDC query showing no committee (S6).

measures.what_it_does: Raises Whatcom County Fire District 1's regular property tax rate to $1.48 per $1,000 for collection in 2027, then lets the levy grow up to 6% a year for nine years. The district serves Everson, Nooksack, Deming and the Nooksack Indian Tribe. Voters narrowly rejected the identical measure in August.
measures.cost_line: Up from about $1.12 to $1.48 per $1,000: about $180 a year more on a $500,000 property. After 2027 the levy may grow up to 6% a year for nine years.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Anne Isenhart) says the 1% growth limit has let the rate fall from the $1.40 voters approved in 2021 to $1.12 while calls and costs rise, that the district has 10 full-time staff for about 1,100 calls a year, and that 'a levy lid lift is not a new tax.'
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no committee against formed. Voters rejected the same proposal in the Aug. 4 primary, 1,744 to 1,620; the fire chief said his impression is that times are tight and the levy would be 'just one more burden.'

taxes.basis: A yes vote raises the regular levy rate from about $1.12 to $1.48 per $1,000, above the $1.40 voters approved in 2021, and allows up to 6% annual growth for nine years.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide records for this measure (S1) and the August Proposition 2026-02 (S2); official August primary results (S3); Cascadia Daily News on the August lid lifts (S4-S6), the 2024 bond attempts (S8, S9) and the new chief (S10); Lynden Tribune on the November rerun (S7); PDC query showing no committee (S11).

measures.what_it_does: Changes Benton City from a mayor-council government, where the elected mayor runs the city, to a council-manager government, effective March 1, 2027. The elected council would hire a professional city manager as chief administrator and pick a mayor from among its members to chair meetings.
measures.cost_line: No tax. The statement for says the change adds payroll for a full-time manager, replacing the mayor's role; no salary or cost estimate was published.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (credited to the City of Benton City) says past administrations mismanaged funds and lost development opportunities under growing state regulation, and that a professional manager under the council is needed. Mayor Len Burton says the council would gain oversight of the executive, and that the unpaid mayor's job averages over 50 hours a week.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed, and no opposition committee is registered with the PDC.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7271 (S1); Apple Valley News Now coverage quoting Mayor Len Burton (S2); chapter 35A.13 RCW (S3); PDC committee query (S4). Resolution 2026-49 and council minutes were not found; the city website blocked automated access.

measures.what_it_does: Lifts Benton City's property tax levy to $1.60 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027 to pay for sheriff's patrol and code enforcement. It may then rise with inflation through 2036, never above $1.60, and the 2036 amount becomes the permanent base for later years.
measures.cost_line: $1.60 per $1,000 in 2027, about $480 a year on a $300,000 home (computed). In 2025 the city rate was $0.71 per $1,000 (about $214 on that home), so the increase is about $266 a year (computed from the 2025 rate). The city says it would raise about $400,000 more a year.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for says the 2027 sheriff and code enforcement costs exceed the city's roughly $301,000 in property tax revenue by about $398,000. It says the sheriff's contract rises 3% a year while property tax revenue can grow only 1%, and that the levy keeps current services without adding programs. A committee with Mayor Len Burton as treasurer supports it.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed, and no opposition committee is registered with the PDC.

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a levy lid lift that more than doubles the city's regular levy rate, from $0.71 (2025) to $1.60 per $1,000. It allows CPI growth through 2036 and keeps the higher amount as the base afterward.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7272 (S1); Department of Revenue levy detail for 2005, 2015, 2020, 2024 and 2025 (S2-S6); RCW 84.55.050 (S7); PDC committee query (S8); Apple Valley News Now identifying the mayor (S9). Resolution 2026-50 and the city budget were not found; no news coverage of the measure was found.

measures.what_it_does: Restores Kiona-Benton City School District's expired educational programs and operations levy for 2027 and 2028. It pays for athletics, arts, technology support, class sizes, nurses, counselors, safety and security, advanced courses and activities. With the state matching money it unlocks, it is about 11% of the district budget.
measures.cost_line: Estimated $1.30 per $1,000 of assessed value: $2,208,341 in 2027 and $2,318,758 in 2028. That is about $390 a year on a $300,000 home (computed). The district puts it at $576 a year on an average $443,267 property. The levy collected in 2025 was $1.29 per $1,000.
measures.pro_summary: The school board says two levy failures led to more than $3 million in cuts and lost teachers. It says passage would bring back counselors, support staff and athletics transportation, and make the district eligible for about $804,000 in state matching funds. A committee, KiBe Kids Yes!, is registered in favor.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed, and no opposition committee is registered with the PDC. Voters rejected $1.50 versions of this levy twice in 2025, by 50 votes in February and 34 in November.

taxes.basis: A yes vote reinstates the expired EP&O levy at $1.30 per $1,000, close to the $1.29 collected in 2025 and below the $1.50 rejected twice in 2025. It is a replacement, not a new kind of tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7273 (S1); district levy page (S2); Secretary of State results for February 2025, November 2025 and February 2023 (S3-S5); Department of Revenue levy detail for 2024-2025 (S6, S7); Apple Valley News Now, NBC Right Now and NewsTalk 870 coverage of cuts, state oversight and the lower rate (S8-S10); PDC committee query (S11). Tri-City Herald coverage could not be retrieved.

measures.what_it_does: Renews the Mount Vernon Transportation Benefit District's 0.2% sales and use tax for ten more years. The money can only pay for transportation work in the city: street repair and maintenance, road capital projects, and bike and pedestrian improvements. The current tax, approved by voters in 2016, ends in spring 2027 unless renewed.
measures.cost_line: Keeps the existing 0.2% (20 cents on a $100 purchase); Mount Vernon's combined sales tax stays at 9.0%. The city estimates $2.3 million a year.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Mount Vernon Transportation Benefit District Pro Committee, spokesperson LuAnne Gordan Burkhart) says the tax pays only for transportation, visitors share the cost, and the city is simply asking to continue it at the same rate. It credits the tax with matching grants and with work on the College Way/I-5 interchange, the Hoag Road/LaVenture signal, street overlays and 436 crosswalks and curbs.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; nobody contacted the Auditor to write one. Councilmember Andrew Vander Stoep voted to put it on the ballot but said he would not support the tax, calling sales tax 'a pretty regressive tax.'

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews an existing 0.2% sales tax at the same rate for ten more years (about $2.3 million a year); the combined rate stays at 9.0%. This is a same-rate renewal, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Skagit County local voters' pamphlet page 18 (S1) and VoteWA record 7426 (S2); the city's ballot filing (S3); the city's Transportation Benefit District page and FAQ (S4); Skagit Valley Herald coverage of the council vote and the 10-year project summary (S5, S6); DOR sales tax rates (S7); 2016 election results (S8); a PDC query showing no committee (S9).

measures.what_it_does: Annexes the City of Sedro-Woolley into the Central Skagit Library District, which already runs the city's library under a contract. City residents would pay the library district's property tax directly instead of the city paying the district, and could vote on library district ballot measures starting in 2027.
measures.cost_line: Library district tax of about $0.232 per $1,000 starting in 2028 (about $517,000 from city property). The city says it will cut its own levy by up to $474,115 to offset most of this, for a net increase of about $11 a year on a $519,450 home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (spokesperson Millissa Macomber) says annexation simplifies library funding because residents already pay for the library through the city. It says the council has committed to lowering city property taxes, and that a yes vote gives residents a say on future library bonds or levies.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; nobody contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote puts a new library district property tax (about $0.232 per $1,000) on city property. The city's offsetting cut of up to $474,115 is its stated commitment for 2028, not part of a permanent rate, and leaves a net increase of about $11 a year on a $519,450 home. A small net increase, like other annexations into an existing taxing district.

local-control.basis: A yes vote moves library funding from a city-negotiated contract into a separate district that sets its own levy, and gives city residents a vote in that district in exchange. Like the King County Fire District 43 annexation, it formalizes an existing service relationship rather than changing who provides the service.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Skagit County local voters' pamphlet page 19 (S1) and VoteWA record 7427 (S2); Resolution No. 1191-26 (S3); the city's library annexation page (S4); the Central Skagit Library annexation FAQ (S5); Skagit Valley Herald coverage (S6, S7); a PDC query showing no committee (S8). The city and the Herald link annexation to a possible future library levy lid lift; the library's FAQ says the two are unrelated.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes a four-year capital levy (2027-2030) for La Conner School District to replace and upgrade technology systems and modernize existing buildings. The district's plans include replacing aging computers and iPads, improving classroom audio-visual systems and repairing facilities.
measures.cost_line: About $0.31 per $1,000 of assessed value each year: $350,000 in 2027 rising to $395,000 in 2030, $1.49 million in total. That is about $154 a year on a $500,000 property.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. Board President Susie Deyo has said the district has been conservative about raising taxes but that the levy is necessary. Board members say upgrading technology before it fails is more efficient.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; nobody contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a four-year capital levy of about $0.31 per $1,000 ($1.49 million total). No expiring capital or technology levy is named; the last La Conner technology levy found on the ballot failed in 2016. It is a new line on current bills, but modest and temporary, like the King precedent for Highline's technology levy.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Skagit County local voters' pamphlet page 20 (S1) and VoteWA record 7428 (S2); Resolution No. 26-14 (S3); Skagit Valley Herald coverage of board meetings (S4-S6); February 2016 election results (S7); a PDC query showing no committee (S8).

measures.what_it_does: Raises Skagit County Fire District 5's regular property tax levy to $0.78 per $1,000 for 2027, up from about $0.34. It then allows revenue growth of up to 3% a year for five years, and the 2031 levy becomes the permanent base. The all-volunteer district serves Allen, Bow, Edison, Samish Island and Chuckanut Drive and plans to use the money mainly to replace aging fire apparatus.
measures.cost_line: $0.78 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027, up from about $0.3363. The district estimates the increase at about $133 a year on a $300,000 home and $222 a year on a $500,000 home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Citizens for District 5 Fire Levy, spokesperson Andrea Leebron-Clay) says the volunteer department faces rising engine, equipment, fuel and operating costs that the 1% limit has not kept up with. It says the levy protects the area's fire protection rating and helps homeowners avoid insurance premium spikes.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; nobody contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote more than doubles the district's regular levy rate (about $0.3363 to $0.78 per $1,000), allows 3% annual revenue growth for five years and makes the 2031 levy the permanent base. That is a large lid lift, like the Spokane Fire District 9 precedent.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Skagit County local voters' pamphlet page 21 (S1) and VoteWA record 7429 (S2); Resolution No. 2026-1 (S3); the district's levy fact sheet (S4); its Reports & Maps and Leadership pages (S5, S6); the PDC record for Citizens for District 5 Fire Levy (S7) and a 2026 PDC query (S8).
