measures.what_it_does: Lifts Longview's regular property tax levy to fund fire and EMS: a third fire station (Station 83 on Ocean Beach Highway), a fourth engine, eight more firefighter paramedic/EMTs and replacement equipment. The 2027 levy becomes the base for future years, with no end date.
measures.cost_line: Adds $1.15 per $1,000 of assessed value from 2027, about $32 a month for a median Longview home by the city's estimate; opponents say the city rate rises from $1.955 to $3.105.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (chair Brad Hannig, the fire chief, with Karen Bergquist and Shannon McLain) says call volume has doubled in 20 years on the same two 1970s stations and staffing, seconds matter in fires and cardiac arrests, and the money is legally restricted to fire and EMS.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (chair Erik Wrzesinski) calls it a permanent 58.8% rate increase on top of a new school levy and higher water rates, and asks the city to return with firm costs and a limited-duration measure.

taxes.basis: A yes vote permanently raises the city's regular property tax rate by $1.15 per $1,000, a new increase rather than a renewal.

spending.basis: The levy funds an explicit expansion of fire and EMS service: a third station, a fourth engine, eight more firefighter paramedic/EMTs and daily staffing raised from nine to 12.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Cowlitz County local voters' pamphlet pp. 57-58 (S1); VoteWA voters' guide record 7372 (S2); City of Longview Prop 1 page (S3); KLOG on the council vote, the open house and the 2025 fire-district proposal (S4-S6, S9); PDC SAFE Longview committee record (S7); sample ballot (S8).

measures.what_it_does: Asks voters for their advice on whether the county commissioners should adopt a new 0.1% countywide sales tax for mental health and chemical dependency treatment and therapeutic courts (RCW 82.14.460). The vote does not impose the tax; the commissioners can adopt it by ordinance without a vote and will decide afterward.
measures.cost_line: If the commissioners later adopt it: 10 cents on a $100 purchase, raising Grant County rates from 8.2-8.5% to 8.3-8.6%. The county projects about $2.7 million a year.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (no author listed) says a modest tax would expand mental health care, substance use treatment, therapeutic courts and crisis services. It says Grant County is the largest of only 10 counties not using this option, and that early treatment eases pressure on police, emergency services and courts.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed, and no opposing committee is listed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote advises the commissioners to adopt a new 0.1% countywide sales tax raising about $2.7 million a year. The vote is advisory, which is the case for a weaker lean.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7349 (S1); county Resolution No. 26-046-CC (S2); the official sample ballot (S3); Columbia Basin Herald on the advisory vote and its $2.7 million estimate (S4); RCW 82.14.460 (S5); DOR Q4 2026 rates (S6); Source ONE News on Renew's mental health capacity (S7); PDC query showing no committee (S8).

measures.what_it_does: Lets the hospital district that runs McKay Healthcare & Rehabilitation in Soap Lake issue up to $9.94 million in bonds over as long as 30 years. The money helps build a 16-bed assisted living unit, a 16-bed memory care unit and a community wellness center with daycare. The district says grants and low-interest loans cover most of the cost. Needs 60% to pass.
measures.cost_line: About $0.61 per $1,000 of assessed value, roughly $15.27 a month ($183 a year) on a $300,000 home, for up to 30 years. The district has had no bond levy before.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (no author listed; the Team McKay committee supports it) says most people over 65 will need skilled care. It says the bond keeps that care close to home, adds child daycare and elder respite, and creates jobs. It notes McKay has served the area since 1938 without a bond.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed, and no opposing committee is listed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a new excess property tax of about $0.61 per $1,000 for up to 30 years to repay up to $9.94 million in bonds. The district has no existing bond levy.

spending.basis: A yes vote helps build new senior-care capacity, a 16-bed assisted living unit, a 16-bed memory care unit and a community wellness center with daycare, an expansion beyond the district's current services.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7343 (S1); the official sample ballot (S2); McKay's expansion page (S3); Columbia Basin Herald coverage (S4); district commission minutes from February to June 2026 on Resolution 2026-4, the USDA loan and grant efforts (S5-S9); Fire District 7 minutes on the same-ballot timing (S10); RCW 70.44.110 and 84.52.056 (S11, S12); the PDC registration of Team McKay (S13).

measures.what_it_does: Creates a new 0.1% city sales and use tax in Moses Lake for police and other public safety and criminal justice services (RCW 82.14.450), with no stated end date. The city says the money would keep current police staffing amid a budget deficit. The city keeps 85% and Grant County gets 15%.
measures.cost_line: Adds 10 cents to a $100 taxable purchase, raising Moses Lake's sales tax from 8.5% to 8.6%. The city estimates about $1.2 million in 2027.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (no author listed) says the police department expects three vacancies in 2026 that it won't fill because of budget cuts. It calls a sales tax one of the most equitable ways to fund police because visitors, shoppers and people outside city limits share the cost, and it does not apply to groceries or gasoline.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed, and no opposing committee is listed. During budget talks, two council members said they preferred cuts and efficiencies to new taxes.

taxes.basis: A yes vote creates a new 0.1% sales tax with no stated end date, raising the combined rate from 8.5% to 8.6% and about $1.2 million a year.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7347 (S1); the city's filed ballot resolution (S2); Columbia Basin Herald on the 7-0 council vote (S3); Source ONE News on the resolution, the city survey, the deficit and the budget plan (S4-S7); DOR Q4 2026 rates (S8); RCW 82.14.450 (S9); PDC query showing no committee (S10).

measures.what_it_does: Replaces the last two years of Fire District 7's 2022 EMS levy ($0.25, suspended since 2024) with a new six-year EMS levy of up to $0.50 per $1,000, collected 2027 through 2032. If it fails, the district resumes the $0.25 levy for 2027 and 2028. The money pays for ambulance staff and equipment in the Soap Lake area.
measures.cost_line: Up to $0.50 per $1,000, at most $150 a year on a $300,000 property, about $250,000 a year for the district. That is $75 a year more than the $0.25 levy that resumes if the measure fails.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The fire chief says EMS calls nearly doubled since 2023, that two EMS positions lose their federal grant in 2027, and that the levy would keep both and add an ambulance.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed. At a June board meeting one resident said he supports the levy but worried that it and the McKay bond on the same ballot could prompt no votes.

taxes.basis: A yes vote doubles the voter-approved EMS rate from $0.25 to $0.50 per $1,000 and extends it four years beyond the 2022 levy. The district had suspended EMS collections since 2024 after a 2023 lid lift. Legally a replacement levy, which is the case for +1.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7348 (S1); the district's Resolution No. 07082026-A (S2); Columbia Basin Herald coverage (S3, S4); VoteWA records and Secretary of State results for the 2022 EMS levy and 2023 lid lift (S5-S8); district board minutes from March to August 2026 (S9-S13); RCW 84.52.069 (S14); PDC query showing no committee (S15).

measures.what_it_does: Renews the Wilson Creek cemetery district's yearly maintenance levy for 2027, which pays its maintenance worker, utilities and mower costs. Voters have approved it every year. Needs 60% to pass.
measures.cost_line: $12,000 in 2027 at about 17.6 cents per $1,000 (about $53 on a $300,000 property). The 2024-2026 levies were $11,500 each.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The district says the levy pays for its maintenance worker, electricity, mower fuel and repairs.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed, and no opposing committee is listed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews a recurring one-year cemetery levy at about the same rate as 2026, with the amount up $500 to $12,000. It is a replacement, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7346 (S1); district Resolution No. 26-1 (S2); VoteWA records for the 2024-2026 levies (S3-S5); Secretary of State results for 2022-2025 (S6-S9); RCW 68.52.310 and 84.52.052 (S10, S11); PDC query showing no committee (S12). No news coverage was found.

measures.what_it_does: A non-binding advisory vote asking voters in unincorporated Island County whether county commissioners should amend county code to ban consumer fireworks there. It does not change the law, and permitted public displays are not affected. Residents of Oak Harbor, Coupeville and Langley do not vote on it. Under state law a ban the board adopted could not take effect for at least a year.
measures.cost_line: No tax or fee. The roughly $3,000 to $3,500 cost of placing it on the ballot was raised by Safe and Humane Fireworks of Island County at the commissioners' request.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Committee for a Safer, Healthier, and more Environmentally Friendly July 4th) cites wildfire risk in a fourth drought-emergency year, limited evacuation routes and volunteer fire departments, 'fireworks tourism,' insurance costs, and harm to animals, veterans and the environment. The Safe & Humane Fireworks Campaign committee reported $11,560 raised.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Committee to Keep Fireworks, written by Commissioner Jill Johnson according to the South Whidbey Record) says current limits on days, mortars and dry-weather bans are a reasonable compromise that should be enforced rather than replaced with prohibition. No opposition committee is registered with the PDC.
measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7304 (S1); Resolution C-62-25 (S2); Island County Code chapter 9.08A (S3) and county fireworks page (S4); RCW 70.77.395 and 70.77.250 (S5, S6); South Whidbey Record coverage (S7-S10); PDC committee and contribution data (S11, S12). No rubric measure axis covers a fireworks ban, so no Lean is shown.

measures.what_it_does: A levy lid lift that permanently raises the City of Langley's regular property tax rate to $1.66 per $1,000 of assessed value starting in 2027, to fund general city services and update the city's technology. After 2027 the levy grows by the usual 1% a year plus new construction from the higher base. Qualifying seniors and people with disabilities are exempt.
measures.cost_line: $1.66 per $1,000, up $0.648544721 from $1.0106789, about a 64% increase in the city's rate (computed). The city puts it at about $42 a month, or $500.50 a year, on the average $770,000 home; computed from the exact rate it is about $499 a year, and about $324 a year on a $500,000 home (computed). The South Whidbey Record reported city property tax collections would rise from about $492,000 to about $808,000 a year.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (credited to the City of Langley) says the city has not sought a lid lift in more than 20 years, that this is 'not a budget expansion' but funding for essential services, and that without it the general fund runs a deficit by 2028. The city says it has already cut services and left jobs unfilled. A committee, Langley Citizens for the Levy, is registered with the PDC.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Committee for Fair Tax Increase in Langley) calls a 65% increase 'just too large,' says Island County could provide some services more cheaply, and says money spent on tourism could cover much of it. The authors say they support a smaller increase. No opposition committee is registered with the PDC.

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a permanent levy lid lift raising the city rate about 64%, from $1.01 to $1.66 per $1,000, about $499 a year on the average home, and city officials say more lifts are likely.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7305 (S1); city levy FAQ (S2) and 2026 budget (S3); South Whidbey Record coverage (S4-S7); Department of Revenue levy detail 2005-2025 (S8-S13); RCW 84.55.050 and chapter 35.07 RCW (S14, S15); PDC committee query (S16). The dossier finds a local-control argument in the campaign statements but notes the measure moves no authority, so no local-control mapping is made; spending is mixed.

measures.what_it_does: A levy lid lift that raises the Port of South Whidbey's property tax rate by six cents, to $0.169 per $1,000, starting in 2027, and keeps the higher amount as the base for later years. The money goes to renovating and modernizing port facilities, including the fairgrounds and waterfront, economic development and expanding the small business incubator program.
measures.cost_line: $0.169 per $1,000, up from $0.109, about a 55% increase in the port's rate (computed). The port puts it at about $4.33 a month, or $52 a year, on the average $866,000 South Whidbey home; about $30 a year on a $500,000 home (computed). The port published no revenue estimate; at 2025 assessed values six cents would raise about $483,000 a year (computed).
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (no author named in the voters' guide) says the levy would help preserve public waterfronts, fairgrounds and small business spaces, address growing maintenance needs and let the port compete for grants that stretch local tax dollars. The port says the rate would return to roughly its 2017 level and that it has cut staff and raised fees.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; the voters' guide says no community members came forward to write one. No opposition committee is registered with the PDC.

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a levy lid lift that raises the port rate six cents, about $52 a year on the average home, and keeps the higher base. The new rate restores the port to below its 2017 rate of $0.183, so it is a modest increase rather than a large one.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7306 (S1); port levy FAQ (S2), June 2026 press release (S3) and June 9 meeting packet (S4); South Whidbey Record coverage (S5-S7); Department of Revenue levy detail 2005-2025 (S8-S14); RCW 84.55.050 (S15); PDC committee query (S16). The signed resolution and vote count were not found. Spending is mixed (preservation versus a new incubator and ferry dock), so it is not mapped.

measures.what_it_does: Lifts Timberland Regional Library's regular property tax levy from about $0.22 to $0.35 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 and 2028; the 2028 amount becomes the base for later limits. TRL says about 96% of its revenue comes from this levy and that the money would restore open hours, staffing and collections after 2026 budget cuts. It is decided by voters across all five TRL counties.
measures.cost_line: From $0.228924 to $0.35 per $1,000 of assessed value, about $14 million more districtwide in 2027. TRL estimates $46 a year on the $357,400 median Lewis County home; the explanatory statement gives about $40 a year on a $334,000 home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for says the levy has not risen in 25 years and has been eroded by rising costs, and that approval would restore hours and staffing and expand collections: 'a long overdue cost-of-living raise.' Former TRL trustees, two from Lewis County, warn that small rural branches could go unstaffed if it fails.
measures.con_summary: The statement against says owners already face rising levy bills and that the library should first cut costs, seek grants and manage existing money better; it says a no vote 'is not a vote against libraries or literacy.' Commissioner Sean Swope questioned why voters able to afford one tax increase should choose the library over schools or public safety.

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a levy lid lift, which the taxes pole_b names explicitly: it raises TRL's regular levy rate by more than half, from $0.228924 to $0.35 per $1,000, about $14 million more in 2027.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide record 7284 (S1); Lewis County sample ballot (S2) and TRL resolution filing (S3); TRL levy page (S4); Chronicle coverage of the commissioners' briefing and the ballot measures, and a former trustees' opinion piece (S5-S7); PDC query (S8). The Lewis guide's for and against statements carry no author names.

measures.what_it_does: Renews the Chehalis Transportation Benefit District's 0.2% sales and use tax for ten more years, July 1, 2027 to June 30, 2037, for street, bridge, sidewalk and traffic-safety work and as local match for grants. The current tax, approved in 2017, expires June 30, 2027 if the renewal fails.
measures.cost_line: 0.2% sales tax (2 cents on a $10 purchase), the current rate, continued for ten years. The city reports about $11.2 million collected since 2017.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for says it is 'not a new tax' and keeps the current rate, and that the money has rebuilt streets and sidewalks and matched about $12.9 million in state and federal grants. Planned uses include Safe Routes to School, the Chamber Way rail bridge and the downtown rejuvenation plan.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no opposition committee was found. In 2017, 45% of Chehalis voters rejected the original tax.

taxes.basis: A yes vote keeps a 0.2% local sales tax that would otherwise expire in 2027 for ten more years. It renews the current rate rather than raising it, so the mapping is +1, not +2.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide record 7365 (S1); TBD resolution filing (S2); SOS February 2017 results (S3); Chronicle coverage and a letter from a downtown business owner (S4-S7); PDC query (S8). The City of Chehalis website refused scripted access.

measures.what_it_does: Sets Fire District 6's regular property tax levy at $1.15 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 collection, for fire and emergency medical service, equipment and apparatus replacement and firefighter safety; that amount becomes the base for later 1%-limited growth. The district serves rural Chehalis and Adna and lost about $193,000 a year when Chehalis annexed part of it in 2026.
measures.cost_line: $1.15 per $1,000 of assessed value, up from about $0.73-$0.79 now (about $0.99 after the annexation). The district's flyer puts the difference at $126 a year on a $300,000 property measured from $0.73; against the $0.99 rate expected without the measure it is about $48.
measures.pro_summary: The district says the fire levy has not had a lid lift in more than 20 years, that call volume has grown, and that the measure is needed to keep current staffing and response times, replace aging apparatus and cover revenue lost to the Chehalis annexation. No statement for was filed in the voters' guide.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no opposition committee was found.

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a levy lid lift that raises the district's fire levy rate by roughly half, from about $0.73-$0.79 to $1.15 per $1,000, and resets the base for later years.

measures.sources_note: VoteWA voters' guide record 7366 (S1); district levy flyer and home page (S2, S3); Chronicle coverage of the measures and of the Fire District 5/6 joint-chief search and annexation settlement (S4, S5); resolution filing (S6); PDC query (S7). The explanatory statement ($0.79) and the district's flyer ($0.73) give different current rates.

measures.what_it_does: Raises Franklin County Fire District 3's property tax levy to $1.24 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 to fund fire and ambulance operations. The 2027 amount becomes the permanent base for later years' levy limits.
measures.cost_line: $1.24 per $1,000 in 2027, up from $0.86 (district figure), about $152 more a year on a $400,000 home (computed).
measures.pro_summary: The district says calls have risen sharply over five years and overlap 30% of the time, slowing response. It says the levy would add a firefighter-paramedic, two seasonal wildland firefighters, gear, ambulance replacements and backup power at the main station. No one filed a pamphlet statement for.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no committee is registered. Voters in the district rejected a similar lift, to $1.28, in August 2024 with 56.9% voting no.

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a permanent levy lid lift, raising the district's regular property tax rate by $0.38 per $1,000 (about 44%) and resetting the base for future limits.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Franklin County local voters' pamphlet, printed page 58 (S1); NonStop Local coverage of the 2026 and 2024 requests (S2, S3); Secretary of State results for the August 2024 primary (S4); RCW 84.55.050 and 52.16.130 (S5, S6); PDC filer list (S7). The district's own website and Resolution No. 491 were not retrieved.

measures.what_it_does: Lets Wenatchee School District borrow $275 million in bonds, repaid by property taxes over up to 20 years. The money replaces most of Wenatchee High School with new classrooms on the same campus, renovates its gyms, pool and auditorium, and installs new HVAC at four elementary and three middle schools. Approval also qualifies the district for an estimated $83 million in state matching funds. Needs 60% to pass.
measures.cost_line: The district estimates $1.46 per $1,000 of assessed value a year for 20 years, about $584 a year on a $400,000 home. This is on top of the current $2.77 school rate. It projects about $444 million repaid in total, including about $169 million in interest.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Chuck Largent, Debbie Walter and Katie Pauly) says the 1972 high school's HVAC can't filter wildfire smoke or cool the building, which causes lost school days, and that its windowless classrooms limit teaching. It says reusing the gyms, pool and auditorium saves over $20 million and that a yes vote unlocks $83 million in state funds.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (the Save Wenatchee High School committee: Bill Sullivan, Mike Dechaney and Cynthia Adams) says a $275 million debt ($440-444 million with interest) is not justified as enrollment falls. It points to the district's 2022 budget error and the 2024 Columbia Elementary closure, and calls for repairing and renovating the existing school instead.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a new 20-year excess property tax of about $1.46 per $1,000, $275 million plus about $169 million in interest, while the 2014 bond is still being repaid.

measures.sources_note: Sources: the county voters' pamphlet pages 16-17 (S1, S2) and VoteWA record 7302 (S3); the district's bond page and FAQ (S4); Wenatchee World and NCWLIFE coverage of the board's decision (S5-S7); the Chelan County Assessor's 2026 levy report (S8); news coverage of the 2022 budget error, the 63 position cuts and the Columbia Elementary closure (S9-S12); the 2026-27 budget (S13); OSPI enrollment counts (S14); a PDC query (S15); NCWLIFE on the Clean Buildings fine (S16).

measures.what_it_does: Raises the City of Cashmere's property tax above the state's 1% yearly growth limit to keep paying for city services. The city's ordinance names law enforcement (the city contracts with the Chelan County Sheriff), fire protection and disaster mitigation. The rate rises to $1.5737 per $1,000 in 2027, and it can grow up to 9% a year from 2028 to 2032. The 2032 level becomes the permanent base for later years.
measures.cost_line: $1.5737 per $1,000 in 2027, up about 13 cents from $1.4441 in 2026: about $52 more a year on a $400,000 home, or roughly $72,000 more for the city. After that, up to 9% more a year through 2032.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The council's ordinance says revenue under the 1% limit will not cover the public services the community needs, including law enforcement, fire protection and disaster mitigation, and that a multi-year lift lets the city plan ahead.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed, and no opposing committee is listed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote lifts the city's levy above the 1% limit, about 9% higher in 2027. It also allows up to 9% yearly increases through 2032 that become the permanent base.

measures.sources_note: Sources: the county voters' pamphlet page 18 (S1) and VoteWA record 7301 (S2); City of Cashmere Ordinance No. 1345 (S3); the Chelan County Assessor's 2026 levy report (S4); the Sheriff's Office patrol page listing contract cities (S5); the June 8, 2026 council agenda (S6); Wenatchee World on Cashmere's jail costs (S7); RCW 84.55.050 (S8); a PDC query showing no committee (S9).

measures.what_it_does: Adds a charter rule that each county commissioner hold at least one town hall a year in their own district, and that the three commissioners together hold at least one a year in each of the three districts. All must be outside normal business hours, with 30 days' notice. Placed on the ballot by the 2025 elected Charter Review Commission.
measures.cost_line: No tax or fee; no fiscal statement was filed.
measures.pro_summary: Charter Review Commission member Ron Richards writes that regular meetings are held at the Port Angeles courthouse during working hours, far from outlying areas, and that commissioners do not answer questions during public comment. Required town halls outside working hours would let people get answers and build confidence in county government.
measures.con_summary: Commission member Jim Stoffer writes that town halls are valuable but do not belong in the charter. Commissioners already hold them, and the amendment does not define a town hall, guarantee answers, or define normal working hours or where notice must be posted.
measures.sources_note: Sources: the printed pamphlet, pages 42-43 (S1, S2); VoteWA record 7289 (S3); the filed resolution packet (S4) and CRC2025-003 (S5); the county's Charter Review Commission page (S6); Peninsula Daily News on the commission's election and the August 2026 debate (S7, S8); the commissioners' July 2026 press release (S9); the charter (S10); a PDC query showing no committee (S11).

measures.what_it_does: Creates a three-member, unpaid county Ethics Review Board, one member per commissioner district. The Auditor, Treasurer, Assessor and Community Development Director appoint members in rotation. The board reviews sworn, first-hand complaints that elected county officials broke the county ethics code and posts written findings online. It cannot impose penalties or look at conduct before the amendment takes effect.
measures.cost_line: No tax or fee, and members serve without pay. No fiscal statement was filed; opponents say staff, legal and records work would cost money.
measures.pro_summary: Andrea Williams writes that some actions by officials are unethical though not illegal. An independent, advisory board would publicly review complaints and give officials guidance, strengthening public trust. (After an August forum she asked to withdraw the statement, then decided to keep it.)
measures.con_summary: Cindy Kelly writes that state law, PDC disclosure, recall and elections already provide accountability. She says the board could become a costly, politicized process that duplicates oversight and diverts staff and funds. Commission member Alex Fane made similar points at a public debate.
measures.sources_note: Sources: the printed pamphlet, pages 44-45 (S1, S2); VoteWA record 7290 (S3); the filed packet, including the committee's August emails (S4); CRC2025-004 (S5); the county's Charter Review Commission page (S6); Peninsula Daily News on the 2025 survey and the August 2026 debate (S7, S8); charter Section 12.60 (S9); a PDC query showing no committee (S10).

measures.what_it_does: Adds a sentence to the county charter requiring that the full text of every future proposed charter amendment be printed in the local voters' pamphlet, as the state pamphlet does for statewide measures.
measures.cost_line: No tax or fee; no fiscal statement was filed. Supporters say the added printing costs essentially nothing; opponents say the cost is not known.
measures.pro_summary: Commission member Ron Richards writes that the county pamphlet has not always included the full text of charter amendments, and that voters need the precise wording because 'the devil is in the details.' He notes the commission approved the amendment 14-0.
measures.con_summary: Commission member Jim Stoffer writes that state law already requires each measure's text plus a neutral explanation, and the full language is available. He says the risk of an amendment being voided is precautionary, not established law, and that the charter should not dictate pamphlet printing.
measures.sources_note: Sources: the printed pamphlet, pages 46-47 (S1, S2); VoteWA record 7291 (S3); the filed packet (S4) and CRC2025-005 with its findings (S5); the county's Charter Review Commission page (S6); Peninsula Daily News on the August 2026 debate (S7); charter Section 11.20.10 (S8); a PDC query showing no committee (S9).

measures.what_it_does: Lets the Forks school district issue $34 million in bonds, repaid by property taxes over up to 25 years, to replace the 1952 Forks Middle School with one secure building. The district says passing now brings about $21 million in state construction aid and keeps its timber revenue. Needs 60% plus minimum turnout.
measures.cost_line: District estimate: about $1.94 per $1,000 of assessed value, almost $680 a year on a $350,000 home, starting in 2028 as the high school bond is paid off. That bond's rate was $1.34 per $1,000 in 2025.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The district says the building fails current safety, seismic and energy codes, that replacing it costs less than remodeling, and that a November vote captures the most state matching money.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed, and no opposing committee is listed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote authorizes a new 25-year excess property tax, estimated at $1.94 per $1,000, to repay $34 million. The district calls it a replacement for the expiring high school bond, which is the case for +1, but its estimate is above that bond's 2025 rate of $1.34.

measures.sources_note: Sources: the printed pamphlet, page 58 (S1); VoteWA record 7296 (S2); district Resolution No. 10-25/26 (S3); Peninsula Daily News and Forks Forum coverage of the bond and the predesign committee (S4-S6); DOR 2025 levy detail (S7); a PDC query showing no committee (S8).

measures.what_it_does: Raises Fire District 1's regular property tax from about $0.47 to $1.00 per $1,000 for 2027 collection. For the next nine years the levy may grow with West Region inflation (at least 1%) instead of the usual 1% cap, up to the $1.50 legal maximum. Simple majority.
measures.cost_line: $1.00 per $1,000 in 2027, up from about $0.47: roughly $300 a year on a $300,000 property instead of $141, and about $630,000 a year for the district at 2025 values. Inflation-based increases follow through 2035.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The district says inflation has outpaced the 1% limit for years and the levy is needed to keep current fire and EMS service and firefighter safety.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed, and no opposing committee is listed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote more than doubles the district's regular levy rate, from about $0.47 to $1.00 per $1,000, and swaps the 1% growth limit for an inflation-based one for nine years. It stays within the $1.50 statutory cap, which is the case for +1.

measures.sources_note: Sources: the printed pamphlet, page 59 (S1); VoteWA record 7292 (S2); district Resolution No. 26-001 (S3); the Forks Forum (S4); DOR 2025 levy detail (S5); a PDC query showing no committee (S6). No statements for or against were filed.

measures.what_it_does: Creates Clallam 2 Fire-Rescue's first dedicated EMS property tax, up to $0.50 per $1,000 for ten years (collected 2027-2036), on top of its regular levy. The money pays for paramedic staffing and equipment and lets the district stop billing residents for uninsured ambulance costs. The same levy got 54% in August, short of the 60% needed.
measures.cost_line: Up to $0.50 per $1,000 a year for ten years: about $150 a year on a $300,000 home, roughly $1.2 million a year for the district. Needs 60% plus minimum turnout.
measures.pro_summary: Dr. Paul Craven, Kolby Konopaski and Dan McKeen write that the district has paid for paramedic care from its fire levy since 2012. They say calls are up 42% in a decade and often overlap, and the levy would fund more staff and end out-of-pocket ambulance bills for residents.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed, and no opposing committee is listed. Voters rejected the same levy in August (54.2% yes, short of 60%) and an earlier version in 2024.

taxes.basis: A yes vote creates a new ten-year EMS property tax of up to $0.50 per $1,000, about $1.2 million a year. The district's regular levy is already at the $1.50 maximum, so the combined rate could reach $2.00.

spending.basis: A yes vote funds added EMS staffing and a new resident benefit: the statement for says that without the levy 'the district can't hire additional personnel' (S2), the money would staff two response units around the clock and build a capital fund for ambulances and cardiac monitors (S7), and it would end billing residents for uninsured transport costs (S2, S7, S8).

measures.sources_note: Sources: the printed pamphlet, pages 60-61 (S1, S2); VoteWA record 7293 (S3); district Resolution No. 2026-03 (S4); Peninsula Daily News coverage from March to August 2026 (S5-S8); the Aug. 4, 2026 results (S9); the Nov. 2024 lid lift results (S10); DOR 2025 levy detail (S11); a PDC query showing no committee (S12).

measures.what_it_does: Lets the all-volunteer Three Rivers fire district (La Push Road, Quillayute Prairie, Mora) raise its regular property tax from about $0.48 to up to $1.50 per $1,000 for 2027 collection, its first lid-lift request since 2010. The amount levied becomes the base for later years. Simple majority.
measures.cost_line: Up to $1.50 per $1,000 in 2027, up from about $0.48: as much as $450 a year on a $300,000 property instead of $143. District tax revenue would rise from about $38,000 to as much as $119,000 at 2025 values.
measures.pro_summary: Chip Keen and district commissioners Tom Rosmond and Scott Horton write that district expenses have more than doubled since 2010 while tax revenue rose 25%, citing safety-standard costs such as turnout gear rising from $2,000 to $5,000. They say timber income is drying up and the levy keeps the volunteer department able to respond safely.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed, and no opposing committee is listed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote lets the district roughly triple its regular levy, from about $0.48 to up to $1.50 per $1,000, and resets the base for future years. It restores eroded rate authority within the statutory cap and the dollars are small, which is the case for +1.

measures.sources_note: Sources: the printed pamphlet, pages 62-63 (S1, S2); VoteWA record 7294 (S3); district Resolution No. 2026-01 (S4); DOR 2025 levy detail (S5); a PDC query showing no committee (S6). No news coverage was found.

measures.what_it_does: Raises Timberland Regional Library's property tax rate from about $0.22 to $0.35 per $1,000 for 2027 and 2028, after which the 2028 amount becomes the base for later years. The library says the money would restore open hours, staffing and collections after a $3.8 million shortfall in 2026. Decided by the combined vote of all five counties; Ocean Shores is outside the library district.
measures.cost_line: About $34 a year on Grays Harbor's median $263,570 home, per the library ($40 a year on a $334,000 home, per the explanatory statement). About $14 million more districtwide in 2027.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (no author listed in the Grays Harbor guide) says the levy has not increased in 25 years and makes up 96% of the library's budget. It calls the increase a long overdue cost-of-living raise that would restore hours, staffing and collections. Four former trustees wrote that rural branches could go unstaffed if it fails.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (no author listed) calls a no vote a vote for fiscal responsibility at a time of rising property tax bills. It says the library should first show it has cut costs and sought grants and partnerships, and that the tax could crowd out schools and emergency services.

taxes.basis: A yes vote raises the library's regular levy rate by about 13 cents per $1,000, a levy lid lift worth about $14 million more districtwide in 2027.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7284 (S1); TRL's levy page with per-county estimates (S2); Daily World coverage of the board vote, the cuts, the information sessions and the McCleary trustee visit (S3-S5, S7); a former trustees' opinion column (S6); the county assessor's 2026 levy book (S8); RCW 84.55.050 (S9); PDC query showing no Grays Harbor committee (S10).

measures.what_it_does: Raises Montesano's city property tax rate to up to $3.22 per $1,000 starting in 2027 and lets the levy grow up to 5% a year for up to six years. The city calls it a renewal of a 2018 levy approved at $3.22 whose rate has fallen to about $1.70. The fire department says it would add two firefighter/EMTs, keep a two-person crew on 24/7, replace equipment and catch up on deferred building repairs.
measures.cost_line: About $1.52 more per $1,000, about $455 a year on a $300,000 home ($468 on the city's $309,000 example). Roughly $960,000 more a year for the city at 2026 values.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The fire department says city costs rose more than 36% in five years, departments deferred maintenance, and two responders on every call improve patient care and safety. The council adopted the ordinance 6-0.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed, and no opposing committee is listed. Council members said taxes are difficult and the measure will be a hard decision for voters.

taxes.basis: A yes vote nearly doubles the city's regular levy rate, from about $1.70 to up to $3.22 per $1,000, and allows 5% annual growth for up to six years.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7377 (S1); the fire department's Proposition 1 page (S2); the July 14 council packet with the draft ordinance (S3); council minutes from July 14, July 28 and Sept. 8 (S4-S6); Daily World coverage (S7, S8); the county assessor's 2026 levy book (S9); 2017 election results (S10); the 2025 medic unit bond record (S11); RCW 84.55.050 (S12); PDC query showing no committee (S13).

measures.what_it_does: Lets McCleary School District borrow $12.8 million over up to 21 years for a secure entry vestibule, door locks, keycard access, a new fire alarm, HVAC, roof, drainage, parking and playground work at McCleary School. It is a smaller version of a $19.3 million bond that failed in February. Needs 60% to pass.
measures.cost_line: About $1.42 per $1,000, or $426 a year on a $300,000 home, for up to 21 years. The district's current bond tax (about $1.19 per $1,000) appears to end after 2026.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The district says aging roof, HVAC and drainage systems have caused water damage, and that community surveys ranked safety and security as a high priority.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed, and no opposing committee is listed. The larger February bond got 43.45% in Grays Harbor, short of the 60% needed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a 21-year excess property tax of about $1.42 per $1,000 to repay $12.8 million in bonds. The existing bond tax appears to end after 2026, so a no vote means no bond tax from 2027.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7385 (S1); the district's levy and bond page and info-session notice (S2, S3); the February 2026 bond record (S4); Daily World coverage of the February bond and its results (S5, S6); the district's four-year budget plan (S7); the county assessor's 2026 levy book (S8); RCW 84.52.056 (S9); PDC query showing no committee (S10).

measures.what_it_does: Creates a permanent emergency medical services property tax of up to 50 cents per $1,000 for Fire District 1, the mostly volunteer department serving about 3,000 people around Oakville. The district has no EMS levy now and began running its own ambulance transports in 2025. Needs 60% to pass; a permanent EMS levy can be sent back to the ballot by a petition of 15% of voters.
measures.cost_line: Up to $0.50 per $1,000, up to $150 a year on a $300,000 home, with no end date. About $157,000 a year for the district at 2026 values.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. The district says rising property values push its levy rate down while the costs of trucks, ambulances, gear, training and medical calls keep rising.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed, and no opposing committee is listed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote creates a new, permanent EMS property tax of up to $0.50 per $1,000 in a district that has no EMS levy today.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7387, ballot title only (S1); the district's levy page (S2); board agendas and minutes from June and July 2026 (S3-S5); Daily World coverage of the district's ambulances, a congressional visit and a levy coffee (S6-S8); the county assessor's 2026 levy book (S9); 2019 election results (S10); RCW 84.52.069 (S11); PDC query showing no committee (S12).

measures.what_it_does: Resets Fire District 2's regular fire levy to $1.50 per $1,000 for 2027 and 2028 collections, after which the 2028 amount becomes the base for later years. The rate has fallen to about $1.40 under the 1% growth limit. The district, which covers more than 300 square miles outside Aberdeen including Brady and the Wynoochee Valley, says the money keeps career and volunteer staffing, apparatus and equipment.
measures.cost_line: About 10 cents more per $1,000, about $30 a year on a $300,000 home. Voters last set the rate at $1.50 in 2023.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Scotty Stead, chairman, and Sharilyn Everitt) says the district has replaced outdated engines, improved medical and safety equipment and renovated the Brady station and strengthened emergency response, and that a strong fire district protects lives, homes and businesses.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed, and no opposing committee is listed.

taxes.basis: A yes vote restores the regular fire levy from about $1.40 to $1.50 per $1,000, about $30 a year on a $300,000 home. Voters approved the same rate in 2020 and 2023, which is the case for a weaker lean.

measures.sources_note: Sources: VoteWA voters' guide record 7386 (S1); the district's levy page (S2); VoteWA records for the 2023 lid lift, the 2020 levy and the 2024 EMS renewal (S3-S5); Secretary of State results for those votes (S6-S8); Daily World on the district's structure (S9); the county assessor's 2026 levy book (S10); RCW 84.55.050 (S11); PDC query showing no committee (S12).

measures.what_it_does: Lifts Timberland Regional Library's regular property tax levy from about $0.22 to $0.35 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 and 2028; the 2028 amount becomes the base for later limits. TRL says the money would maintain and restore open hours, staffing and collections after 2026 budget cuts. Mason County's branches are in Shelton, Belfair and Hoodsport, and voters in all five TRL counties decide the measure.
measures.cost_line: From $0.228924 to $0.35 per $1,000 of assessed value. TRL estimates $43 a year on the $333,773 median Mason County home; the explanatory statement gives about $40 a year on a $334,000 home.
measures.pro_summary: The TimberStrong Libraries Committee says the levy was last approved more than 25 years ago and has eroded to $0.22, and that approval would restore frontline staff, hours and programs; without it the Hoodsport branch could go unstaffed and Belfair and Shelton could face further cuts.
measures.con_summary: Citizens for Accountable TR Libraries (Sean Swope) says owners already face rising levy bills and the library should first cut costs, seek grants and manage existing money better; 'Voting No is not a vote against libraries or literacy.'

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a levy lid lift, which the taxes pole_b names explicitly: TRL's regular levy rate rises by more than half, from $0.228924 to $0.35 per $1,000.

measures.sources_note: Mason local voters' pamphlet pp. 24-25 (S1) and VoteWA guide record 7284 (S2); TRL levy page (S3); Shelton-Mason County Journal coverage of TRL's 2026 deficit and layoffs, free previews only (S4-S6); PDC committee query (S7). The pamphlet's Mason statement for differs from the generic statement for in the VoteWA guide.

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Southside School District's expiring educational programs and operations levy for four years (2027-2030). The money pays for staffing, health and safety, afterschool programs, curriculum, technology, nutrition and special education costs that state and federal funding do not cover.
measures.cost_line: $994,006 in 2027 rising to $1,217,701 in 2030, an estimated $1.97 per $1,000 of assessed value each year, the same maximum rate voters approved in 2022.
measures.pro_summary: Evelyn and James Huff: the community has long supported the school, founded in 1903 and now serving about 200 students, and 'the students deserve the best we can give them.'
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no opposition committee was found.

taxes.basis: A yes vote continues a school operations levy at the same maximum rate voters approved in 2022 ($1.97 per $1,000); it renews an expiring tax rather than raising the rate, so +1, not +2.

measures.sources_note: Mason local voters' pamphlet pp. 26-27 (S1) and VoteWA guide record 7383 (S2); Shelton-Mason County Journal preview (S3); PDC committee query (S4).

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes McCleary School District to issue $12.8 million in general obligation bonds, repaid over up to 21 years by an excess property tax, for a security vestibule, door locks, keycard access and fire alarms, building, HVAC, drainage and parking repairs, and safer playgrounds at the McCleary School. Only the small part of the district inside Mason County votes on it here.
measures.cost_line: $12.8 million in bonds; the district estimates $1.42 per $1,000 of assessed value, about $426 a year on a $300,000 home.
measures.pro_summary: No statement for was filed. The district says the bond would pay for safety and security improvements and key facility repairs that state grants do not cover; a broader bond failed in February 2026.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no opposition committee was found.

taxes.basis: A yes vote authorizes new bonds repaid by a new excess property tax, estimated at $1.42 per $1,000 for up to 21 years.

measures.sources_note: Mason local voters' pamphlet p. 28 (S1) and VoteWA guide record 7385 (S2); McCleary School District levy and bond pages (S3, S4); PDC committee query (S5).

measures.what_it_does: Replaces Pioneer School District's educational programs and operations levy, which expires after 2027, for four years (2028-2031). It pays for smaller classes, safety and security, mental health specialists, music and STEM, academic supports, athletics and activities the state does not fully fund.
measures.cost_line: $3,700,000 in 2028 rising to $4,043,090 in 2031, an estimated $1.18 to $1.15 per $1,000 of assessed value.
measures.pro_summary: No statement for was filed.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no opposition committee was found.

taxes.basis: A yes vote continues a school operations levy that would otherwise end after 2027; the ballot materials present it as a replacement and give no comparison with the current rate, so +1, not +2.

measures.sources_note: Mason local voters' pamphlet p. 29 (S1) and VoteWA guide record 7382 (S2); Shelton-Mason County Journal preview (S3), whose levy details are paywalled; PDC committee query (S4). The district's website is script-rendered and its levy page could not be read.

measures.what_it_does: Raises the Shelton Transportation Benefit District's sales and use tax from 0.2% to 0.3% for ten years, for street and pedestrian maintenance, repair and construction: safety improvements, ADA compliance, resurfacing, bike and multimodal connections and grant matching. Anyone buying taxable goods in the city pays it.
measures.cost_line: Sales tax for transportation rises from 0.2% to 0.3%, one more cent on a $10 purchase, for ten years; no revenue estimate is given.
measures.pro_summary: No statement for was filed. The City Council voted unanimously in July 2026 to move the increase toward the ballot.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed and no opposition committee was found.

taxes.basis: A yes vote raises a local sales tax rate by half, from 0.2% to 0.3%, for ten years.

measures.sources_note: Mason local voters' pamphlet p. 30 (S1) and VoteWA guide record 7384 (S2); Shelton-Mason County Journal previews on the council's July vote and the 2025 renewal (S3, S4); PDC committee query (S5). The explanatory statement dates the TBD's creation to 2016, the Journal to a November 2015 vote.
